Clinical Reference

Septic Arthritis

On this page
Bacterial infection inside a joint space — a surgical and medical emergency in which the cartilage is destroyed mostly by the host's own neutrophil enzymes, so the joint must be drained as well as sterilised, and it must happen today.
2–12 / 100,000 per year Aspirate BEFORE antibiotics Mortality ~7–15% Permanent joint damage ~1 in 3 Drainage + IV antistaphylococcal cover Hip = same-day OR
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story, told so the treatment becomes obvious

1. The joint is uniquely easy to infect

Synovium is one of the most richly vascularised tissues in the body, and its capillaries lack a limiting basement membrane — an arrangement that exists so nutrients can diffuse freely to the avascular cartilage. In most tissues bacteria have to work to cross the endothelium; in the synovium they essentially fall out of the bloodstream into the joint. This single anatomical fact explains why haematogenous spread is the dominant route, and why a bacteraemia brief enough to be clinically silent — from a skin ulcer, an infected line, a dental procedure or endocarditis — can end up as an infected knee.

Once inside, the bacteria find a hospitable environment. Synovial fluid has low complement and opsonin activity, its high hyaluronan viscosity physically impedes phagocyte movement, and the resident synovial macrophages are outnumbered within hours. The joint is, functionally, a partially immune-privileged pocket.

2. Adhesion — the organism grabs the cartilage

Staphylococcus aureus is the dominant pathogen precisely because it is equipped for this niche. Its MSCRAMMs (Microbial Surface Components Recognising Adhesive Matrix Molecules) — fibronectin-binding proteins A and B, the collagen adhesin Cna, and clumping factors A and B — bind directly to the collagen and fibronectin of exposed cartilage matrix. Strains carrying Cna are substantially more arthritogenic in animal models. Damaged or arthritic cartilage exposes more binding sites, which is a large part of why rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis are risk factors rather than incidental findings.

3. The host response — and the central paradox of this disease

Bacterial peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid engage TLR2; lipopolysaccharide from gram-negatives engages TLR4. Synovial macrophages respond with TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6, and the chemokine gradient pulls an enormous neutrophil population into a space that has nowhere to drain.

Those neutrophils are the problem. They release elastase and cathepsin G; they induce synoviocytes and chondrocytes to secrete matrix metalloproteinases MMP-1, MMP-3 and MMP-13; and they generate reactive oxygen species. S. aureus adds direct injury on top of this — Panton-Valentine leukocidin and α-haemolysin kill chondrocytes outright, and bovine cartilage explant work shows in-situ chondrocyte death is rapid. Cartilage has no vasculature, no nerve supply, and essentially no capacity for repair.

The experimental trajectory is well characterised. In the rabbit S. aureus knee model, glycosaminoglycan content of tibial plateau cartilage has already fallen ~42% at 48 hours; marginal cartilage erosion is visible by day 5; GAG loss reaches ~73% by week 3; and untreated joints proceed to total destruction by about week 5.

You will hear "cartilage is irreversibly damaged within 8 hours" quoted on rounds. That specific figure does not trace to a primary source and is best avoided. What is solidly established is the trajectory above — measurable matrix loss within 48 hours and visible erosion by day 5 — which supports exactly the same conclusion without inventing a number: get source control within 24 hours.
The cartilage damage in septic arthritis is predominantly host-mediated, not bacterial. This is the reason antibiotics alone are inadequate treatment. Sterilising the fluid does nothing about the elastase, MMPs and free radicals already dissolved in it, or about the pressure. Only drainage removes the enzyme load. An antibiotic prescription without a drainage plan is half a treatment.

4. Pressure and ischaemia

The effusion accumulates inside a fibrous capsule with almost no compliance. Rising intra-articular pressure tamponades the epiphyseal and synovial vessels. In the hip this is catastrophic: the femoral head's blood supply runs through the retinacular vessels inside the capsule, so a tense septic hip effusion can infarct the femoral head outright. That vascular anatomy — not tradition — is why a septic hip goes to the operating theatre the same day, in adults as in children.

5. Biofilm — and why hardware changes everything

Adherent staphylococci switch to a sessile, slow-metabolising, exopolysaccharide-encased phenotype. Biofilm-embedded organisms tolerate antibiotic concentrations 100–1000× their planktonic MIC, not because of acquired resistance but because they are barely metabolising. In a native joint most of the burden is planktonic and drainage plus systemic antibiotics work. On a prosthesis, biofilm is the disease, and no antibiotic regimen reliably cures it while the implant stays in place — which is why prosthetic joint infection is a fundamentally different problem with a different algorithm.

A sealed aquarium with no drain. Bacteria are a fire lit inside the tank. Antibiotics put the fire out — but the water is now full of ash and acid, and it is the water that is dissolving the glass. Every hour that toxic water sits there, more of the tank lining is gone for good, and the lining does not regrow. Draining and refilling the tank is not an optional extra; it is the part that saves the glass. And if there is a plastic ornament in the tank (a prosthesis), the slime on it re-seeds the water no matter how much chlorine you add — the ornament has to come out.
The cascade from bacterial arrival to permanent cartilage loss. Note that the destructive arm (amber and red) is driven by host effectors — which is why the therapeutic answer has two halves: kill the organism, and physically remove the inflammatory soup.
The therapeutic clock. In experimental S. aureus arthritis, glycosaminoglycan content of the tibial plateau has already fallen ~42% at 48 hours, marginal erosion is visible by day 5, GAG loss reaches ~73% by week 3, and untreated joints are destroyed by about week 5. There is no validated "hours to permanent damage" number in humans — but every published trajectory says the same thing: this is a same-day problem, not a review-in-the-morning problem.
The synovial joint. The synovial membrane lining the capsule is the vascular route in; the articular cartilage is the avascular, non-regenerating structure being destroyed. Note there is no lymphatic drainage path for pus to leave a closed joint — it has to be taken out.
OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file
Purulent synovial fluid aspirated from a septic joint. This is the "toxic water" of the analogy made literal — a syringe full of neutrophils, elastase, MMPs and free radicals. Antibiotics will sterilise it; only drainage removes it. Note that fluid this obviously abnormal still goes for cell count, Gram stain and culture: the appearance tells you to treat, the laboratory tells you with what.
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file

6. Tying every therapy to the exact step it interrupts

This table is the through-line of the whole guide. Nothing below is a drug name to memorise — each one is aimed at a specific box in the cascade above.
InterventionStep in the cascade it attacksConsequence if you skip it
Joint drainage
aspiration / arthroscopy / arthrotomy		Physically removes neutrophils, elastase, MMPs, ROS, bacterial load and pressure. The only intervention that addresses the host-mediated arm.Cartilage keeps dissolving on antibiotics. Effusion under pressure keeps tamponading the epiphyseal supply. This is the commonest serious management error in the disease.
Antistaphylococcal β-lactam
cefazolin, nafcillin, oxacillin, flucloxacillin		Binds penicillin-binding proteins → blocks peptidoglycan transpeptidation → bactericidal cell-wall failure. Removes the upstream TLR2 stimulus.Ongoing bacterial replication regenerates the cytokine drive faster than drainage can clear it; bacteraemia continues and seeds elsewhere.
VancomycinBinds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors — a step upstream of PBPs, so it works despite the altered PBP2a of MRSA.MRSA is untreated. In a population where MRSA can exceed 20–25% of staphylococcal isolates, empirically omitting it is a real risk.
CeftriaxoneHigh-affinity binding to gonococcal and gram-negative PBPs; excellent synovial fluid penetration.N. gonorrhoeae and community gram-negatives (often the elderly, urinary-source, or immunocompromised patient) go untreated.
Early mobilisation / CPMCartilage is nourished by cyclical loading and synovial diffusion; motion also prevents adhesion formation between denuded surfaces.Fibrous ankylosis and contracture. Roughly 39% of patients in the Gjika trial had mechanical sequelae — stiffness and adhesions dominate that figure.
Rifampin
only with retained hardware		Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; uniquely active against stationary-phase staphylococci inside biofilm.Biofilm on retained hardware survives. Irrelevant in an ordinary native joint — do not add it reflexively.
NOT intra-articular antibioticsNothing useful — systemic agents already achieve therapeutic synovial fluid concentrations because inflamed synovium is highly permeable.Adds a chemical synovitis that mimics treatment failure and confuses everything. Actively harmful; do not do it.
NOT intra-articular steroid—Suppresses the local response to an active pyogenic infection. Contraindicated in septic arthritis.
Antibiotic penetration into synovial fluid is good for β-lactams, vancomycin, clindamycin, linezolid and fluoroquinolones — inflamed synovium leaks. This is the opposite of the situation in bone or biofilm, and it is why "the drug can't get in" is not a valid reason for treatment failure in a native joint. When a native joint fails to improve, suspect undrained pus, an adjacent osteomyelitis or abscess, the wrong organism, or a resistant organism — not poor penetration.

Classification — the distinctions that change management

Route of entry

RouteShare of casesTypical settingWhat it changes
HaematogenousDominant routeAny bacteraemia: skin/soft-tissue infection, IV drug use, indwelling lines, pneumonia, UTI, endocarditis, dental sepsisAlways ask where did the bacteraemia come from. Draw blood cultures — positive in roughly 25–50%. If S. aureus grows, get an echocardiogram: concurrent endocarditis is not rare and changes duration entirely.
Direct inoculationSecond commonestPenetrating trauma, bites, thorn/splinter injury, open fracture, iatrogenic (injection, arthroscopy)Organism follows the mechanism: Pasteurella multocida after a cat bite, Eikenella corrodens after a human bite/fight-bite, Pseudomonas after a puncture through footwear, Sporothrix after a rose thorn. Retained foreign body must be excluded.
Contiguous spreadLess commonAdjacent osteomyelitis (transphyseal in young children), overlying cellulitis or abscess, diabetic foot ulcerMandates imaging for the bone. If osteomyelitis coexists, duration extends to ~6 weeks and orthopaedic debridement becomes more likely.
Iatrogenic post-injection~0.09–0.18% per injectionIntra-articular corticosteroid or viscosupplementationA 2025 propensity-matched cohort found ~18 per 10,000 large-joint steroid injections (0.18%); a single-centre series found 14/15,021 (0.093%) within 6 months, with median time to diagnosis 3.5 weeks and a bimodal peak at 1–3 and 7–10 weeks. Low absolute risk — but a previously injected joint that turns hot weeks later must be tapped, and outbreaks have been traced to unsafe injection practice.

Gonococcal vs non-gonococcal — genuinely two different diseases

FeatureNon-gonococcal (pyogenic)Gonococcal / disseminated GC infection
Typical patientOlder, comorbid; or IVDU; or prior joint diseaseYoung, sexually active; menstruating and pregnant women and complement-deficient patients over-represented
Joint patternMonoarticular ~80–90%, large joint, knee firstOften migratory polyarthralgia → settles into 1–2 joints; asymmetric; wrists/knees/ankles
Extra-articular cluesSource of bacteraemia (cellulitis, line, endocarditis)Tenosynovitis (highly characteristic) + pustular/vesiculopustular or haemorrhagic skin lesions, usually few and on the extremities
Synovial WBCUsually very high, often >50,000–100,000Often lower — may be in the 20,000–50,000 range
Synovial culturePositive ~40–70%Frequently NEGATIVE (~25–50% at best) — the organism is fastidious and dies in transport
Blood culturePositive ~25–50%Usually negative in the purulent-arthritis form; higher in the early bacteraemic arthritis-dermatitis phase
How you actually prove itSynovial and blood cultureNAAT of urogenital, pharyngeal and rectal sites — do all exposed sites, regardless of symptoms. Synovial fluid NAAT is off-label but often the only positive test.
TreatmentDrainage + organism-directed IV → oral; 3–6 weeksCeftriaxone 1 g IV/IM q24h; oral step-down 24–48 h after substantial improvement; total ≥7 days (CDC 2021). Often needs far less aggressive drainage.

A gonococcal skin lesion in disseminated gonococcal infection. These are typically few in number, pustular or vesiculopustular with a haemorrhagic base, and on the distal extremities — which means you will only find them if you undress the patient and look. Paired with dorsal tenosynovitis in a young sexually active adult, this picture is worth more than the joint culture, which is usually negative.
CDC/Dr. Thomas F. Sellers, Emory University (Public Health Image Library #2038), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons · source file
If your patient is young, sexually active and has tenosynovitis plus a few pustules, send the NAATs and start ceftriaxone even with a sterile joint aspirate — and treat the partner. Conversely, do not let a "classic DGI story" stop you draining a frankly purulent joint. And screen for HIV and syphilis at the same time: they travel together.

Monoarticular vs polyarticular

Around 10–20% of pyogenic cases involve more than one joint. Polyarticular disease is not simply "more of the same" — it signals sustained bacteraemia and a compromised host (rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, endocarditis, IV drug use), and it carries substantially higher mortality. Multiple-joint sepsis was an independent predictor of death in Weston's 10-year UK cohort, alongside confusion at presentation, age ≥65 and elbow involvement.

Two or more septic joints = look hard for the engine driving it. Echocardiogram for endocarditis, examine every line, culture everything. Treating the joints without finding the source guarantees relapse.

Native joint vs prosthetic joint — do not blur these

Native joint septic arthritisProsthetic joint infection (PJI)
Dominant biologyPlanktonic bacteria + host enzymesBiofilm on the implant
Diagnostic synovial WBCTypically >50,000 (but no cut-off excludes)Far lower — chronic PJI thresholds are of the order of >3,000/µL with >65–80% PMN. Applying the native-joint cut-off will make you miss it.
Who aspiratesMedicine/EM/rheumatology at the bedsideThe arthroplasty service — sterile technique matters enormously, and a contaminated tap ruins the diagnostic pathway
Surgical strategyDrain and retain the jointDAIR (debridement, antibiotics, implant retention) only if symptoms are short (roughly <3–4 weeks), the implant is stable and there is no sinus tract; otherwise 1- or 2-stage exchange (IDSA 2013)
Duration~3–6 weeks (see the duration debate)Longer, and rifampin-based combinations for staphylococci with retained hardware. Do not generalise short-course native-joint data to a prosthesis.

Newman criteria — what counts as "definite"

Useful when you are writing the problem list and the culture is negative. Newman's classification defines septic arthritis as present when any one of the following is met:

  • A — organism isolated from the joint
  • B — organism isolated from blood or another site in a patient with a clinically infected joint
  • C — typical clinical features and turbid synovial fluid in a patient already on antibiotics, with negative cultures
  • D — post-mortem or radiographic evidence of joint infection
Category C exists precisely because 10–20% of cases are culture-negative — most often because antibiotics were given before the joint was aspirated. A negative culture in a patient who received a dose of antibiotics in the ED does not un-diagnose septic arthritis. Treat the syndrome.

Presentation

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

sensitivities from Margaretten, JAMA 2007
Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Joint pain~85%The fibrous capsule and synovium are densely innervated by nociceptors; distension by an effusion under pressure plus bradykinin and prostaglandin sensitisation makes it exquisite. Pain is at rest and on the slightest passive movement — that is what separates it from mechanical pain, which needs load. The single most sensitive symptom, but utterly non-specific.
Restricted range of motion / patient holds the joint still~80–90%Reflex muscle guarding to minimise capsular stretch. The joint sits in the position of maximum capsular volume — hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated; knee slightly flexed. A patient who will not let you move the joint at all through a few degrees is telling you something a patient with cellulitis or bursitis will not.
Joint swelling (history of)~78%Cytokine-driven vasodilation and capillary leak produce an inflammatory effusion; the neutrophil mass itself adds volume. Easy to see in the knee, elbow and ankle; invisible in the hip and sacroiliac joint, where deep muscle bulk hides even a large effusion.
Raised CRP and/or ESR~90–95%IL-6 drives the hepatic acute-phase response. The most sensitive laboratory finding and the best marker to trend. Beware: CRP rises within 6–8 h, but ESR lags by days — very early presentations can have a normal ESR with a climbing CRP.
Warmth and erythema over the joint~50–70%Inflammatory hyperaemia. Frequently muted or absent in deep joints (hip, shoulder, SI), in the elderly, and in patients on corticosteroids or biologics. Overlying erythema also raises the competing question of cellulitis — which matters, because you should avoid passing a needle through frankly infected skin if another window exists.
Fever (any)~57%IL-1β and prostaglandin E₂ raise the hypothalamic set-point. Roughly 4 in 10 patients are afebrile. This is the classic trap: the absence of fever does essentially nothing to lower your probability, and it is least reliable in exactly the patients most at risk — the elderly, the immunosuppressed and those on steroids or TNF inhibitors.
Peripheral leukocytosis~50–60%Marrow neutrophil release under G-CSF and IL-6 drive. A normal white count is common and reassuring about nothing. Interpret it alongside the synovial count, never instead of it.
Inability to weight-bear (lower limb)~50–70%Loading compresses the inflamed cartilage and raises intra-articular pressure. One of the four Kocher predictors in children, and a good rough triage sign in adults too.
Rigors / sweats / systemic toxicity~20–30%Reflects intermittent bacteraemia rather than the joint itself. Its presence should send you looking for the source; its absence excludes nothing.
Positive blood cultures~25–50%The joint was usually seeded from the blood, and the bloodstream is often still seeded when the patient arrives. This is exactly why you draw 2 sets before the first antibiotic dose — sometimes the blood is the only thing that grows, and it names the organism for you.
Polyarticular involvement (≥2 joints)~10–20%Sustained bacteraemia seeding multiple synovial beds in a host who cannot contain it. Independently associated with higher mortality; mandates a hunt for endocarditis or an intravascular source.
Tenosynovitis (dorsal wrist/hand, ankle)~one-third of gonococcal casesGonococcal immune complexes and organisms deposit in tendon sheaths as well as synovium. Very suggestive of disseminated gonococcal infection and rare in staphylococcal disease — a genuinely useful discriminator.
Pustular / vesiculopustular or haemorrhagic skin lesions~two-thirds of DGISeptic emboli and immune complex deposition in dermal vessels. Typically few in number (often under 30), on the distal extremities and trunk, and easy to miss unless you undress the patient. Swab or biopsy them — they occasionally grow the organism.
Confusion / delirium at presentation<15%Sepsis-associated encephalopathy, often in an older comorbid patient. An independent predictor of death in Weston's cohort — treat it as a severity marker, not as a distraction from the joint.
Septic shock / hypotension~5–10%Uncommon at presentation because the burden is compartmentalised. When it does occur, look for a large undrained joint, concurrent endocarditis, necrotising soft-tissue infection, or a polyarticular presentation. This is the subgroup that belongs in the unit.
Dry tap (no fluid obtained)~10–20% of attemptsThick fibrinous pus, loculation, a small joint, or a deep joint aspirated blind. A dry tap is not a negative result. Repeat under ultrasound or fluoroscopic guidance, or escalate to the surgeon — do not document "aspiration negative" and move on.

Which joint?

Joint~Share of casesWhat is special about it
Knee~45–55%Largest synovial volume, most superficial, easiest to aspirate and to lavage. The one you will actually tap at the bedside. Serial needle aspiration is a reasonable strategy here.
Hip~15–20%Surgical emergency. Deep, cannot be assessed by inspection, cannot be reliably aspirated blind, and the femoral head's blood supply is intracapsular → avascular necrosis. Image-guided aspiration and same-day theatre.
Shoulder~10%Also deep and hard to drain adequately with a needle; commonly associated with rotator-cuff pathology and prior injection. Usually surgical.
Ankle / wrist / elbow~10–15% combinedAspirable. Wrist and hand joints made up the majority of the Gjika short-course trial, which is why its 2-week result generalises best to small joints.
Sternoclavicular joint<5% overallStrongly associated with injection drug use and indwelling catheters. Always get a CT — it extends into the mediastinum, retrosternal space and chest wall far more often than you would guess, and that changes the operation.
Sacroiliac joint<5%Presents as buttock/low-back pain with fever and a positive FABER — routinely misdiagnosed as mechanical back pain for weeks. Needs MRI or CT; cannot be examined or aspirated conventionally.
Small joints of hand/foot, symphysis pubis, facet joints<5%Bite wounds and penetrating injury for the hand; athletes and pelvic surgery for the symphysis. Facet joint infection mimics vertebral osteomyelitis.
The clinical appearance: a swollen, distended joint held still. Note that erythema and swelling are what you can see — but the diagnosis is never made by looking. It is made with a needle.
James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file
Arthrocentesis — the single most important act in this disease. Aim for the largest, most accessible effusion; avoid traversing cellulitic skin if any alternative window exists; and send the fluid before the first antibiotic dose whenever the patient is stable enough to allow it.

Risk factors — with the numbers where they exist

The most rigorously quantified data come from Kaandorp et al., Arthritis & Rheumatism 1995 — a prospective study of 4,907 rheumatic-disease clinic patients followed 3 years (37 developed septic arthritis). Those odds ratios are given below where available.

Risk factorMagnitudeMechanism
Skin infectionOR 27.2 (95% CI 7.6–97.1)The single strongest association in Kaandorp — and the most actionable, because it is the portal of entry. A cellulitis, ulcer or infected wound anywhere on the body is the bacteraemic source. Examine the whole skin surface, including between the toes and under dressings.
Prosthetic hip or kneeOR 15 (95% CI 4.1–54.3)Biofilm substrate. Different disease, different algorithm — see the native-vs-prosthetic table above.
Recent joint surgeryOR 5.1 (95% CI 2.2–11.9)Direct surgical inoculation plus a breached capsule and a haematoma to grow in.
Rheumatoid arthritisOR 4.0 (95% CI 1.9–8.3); present in ~20% of septic arthritis cohorts vs ~1% of the populationDamaged cartilage exposes collagen binding sites; chronic synovitis means a permanently hyperaemic synovium; and the immunosuppressive treatment compounds it. Critically, the presentation is blunted — often afebrile, and the joint pain gets written off as a flare.
Age ≥80 yearsOR 3.5 (95% CI 1.4–8.6)Immunosenescence, more comorbidity, more gram-negative disease, atypical and afebrile presentation, and delayed diagnosis. 90-day mortality has been reported around 22.7% in patients over 79.
Diabetes mellitusOR 3.3 (95% CI 1.1–10.1); also an independent predictor of morbidity (Weston 1999)Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and oxidative burst; skin and ulcer portals of entry; peripheral neuropathy delays presentation; vascular disease impairs healing.
TNF-α inhibitor therapy4.2 vs 1.8 per 1,000 patient-years; adjusted HR 2.3 (95% CI 1.2–4.4) vs non-biologic DMARDs (BSRBR, Galloway)TNF-α is essential for granuloma formation and neutrophil recruitment. Blocking it impairs early containment of staphylococcal seeding — and also removes the fever that would have alerted you.
Injection drug useMajor (effect size not pooled)Recurrent bacteraemia from non-sterile injection. Distinctive joint distribution — sternoclavicular, sacroiliac, symphysis pubis, spine — and distinctive organisms (S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Candida, polymicrobial). Always get an echocardiogram.
Recent intra-articular injection~0.09–0.18% per injectionDirect inoculation. Low absolute risk, but if a previously injected joint becomes acutely hot — even weeks later — it must be tapped.
Gout / CPPDCoexists in ~1.5–5% of cohorts, up to 21.3% of surgically treated seriesCrystal disease damages cartilage and causes recurrent effusions, both of which raise infection risk. And crystals in the fluid do not rule out infection: the two are genuinely found together, and a crystal-positive result has misled many clinicians into discharging a septic joint.
HIV / malignancy / chemotherapy / chronic steroids / cirrhosis / haemodialysis / sickle cellAll increase riskReduced opsonisation and neutrophil function; recurrent line-associated bacteraemia in dialysis; functional asplenia in sickle cell (encapsulated organisms and Salmonella).
🩺 Clinic — recognition, the right first moves, and what happens after discharge
Assess

When to suspect

⛑️

Read this first — septic arthritis is not an outpatient disease

There is essentially no role for outpatient management of suspected native joint septic arthritis in adults. Every reviewed guideline defaults to admission. Your job in clinic is to recognise it, get the fluid or get them somewhere that can, avoid the three classic errors below, and send them in the same day.
The three clinic errors that cost jointsWhy it is harmfulDo this instead
1. Starting oral antibiotics and reviewing in a few daysSub-therapeutic partial treatment sterilises the culture without curing the joint. Prior antibiotics drop Gram-stain sensitivity from ~58% to ~12% and culture from ~79% to ~28%. You have now taken away the one test that would have named the organism, and the cartilage is still being digested.Send them in undosed. If you genuinely cannot arrange same-day assessment and the patient looks septic, then treat — but say clearly in your referral that antibiotics were given and when.
2. Injecting the joint with corticosteroidYou may be injecting steroid into an active pyogenic infection, and you have introduced a second inoculation risk. There is no role for intra-articular steroid in septic arthritis.If there is any possibility this is infection, aspirate — never inject. Aspiration is diagnostic; injection is a gamble.
3. Accepting "it's just a gout flare" or "it's just her RA"Crystals coexist with infection in up to 21% of surgically treated series, and RA patients make up roughly 20% of all septic arthritis cases while being the group most likely to be afebrile.A previous diagnosis of crystal or inflammatory arthritis raises the risk of septic arthritis. It never lowers it. A single acutely hot joint gets tapped.
🔍

The clinic presentation — and who is in front of you

The classic textbook patient — young, febrile, rigoring, with a hot swollen knee — is the easy one. The patients who get missed are:

  • The elderly comorbid patient who is afebrile, has a "bit more" knee pain, and a raised CRP that gets attributed to their osteoarthritis. Remember: 90-day mortality in the over-79s has been reported around 22.7%.
  • The RA patient on a TNF inhibitor whose single hot joint is booked in as a flare. Adjusted HR 2.3 for septic arthritis on anti-TNF therapy — and the drug removes the fever that would have alerted you.
  • The young sexually active patient with migratory joint pains, a swollen wrist, dorsal tenosynovitis and a handful of pustules they did not mention. This is disseminated gonococcal infection and it will not culture from the joint.
  • The person who injects drugs with buttock, shoulder-girdle or chest pain rather than a peripheral joint — sacroiliac and sternoclavicular disease, often Pseudomonas, and often mistaken for musculoskeletal back pain for weeks.
  • The patient injected 3 weeks ago. Post-injection septic arthritis has a median time to diagnosis of 3.5 weeks and a bimodal peak at 1–3 and 7–10 weeks. The link is easy to miss because it is not immediate.
The most useful bedside discriminator is pain on tiny-amplitude passive movement. Bursitis, cellulitis and tendinopathy allow you to move the joint through a few degrees; a genuinely septic joint does not. Test the hip with gentle log-roll — if that is exquisite, the joint is the problem, not the soft tissue.
Get the whole patient undressed. You are looking for the portal of entry (skin infection carries OR 27.2 — the strongest risk factor in the Kaandorp data), for pustular lesions of DGI, for injection sites, and for a second involved joint. Polyarticular disease changes the mortality estimate several-fold.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The order set — and what each result actually changes

ArthrocentesisTHE test. Before antibiotics, whenever the patient is haemodynamically stable. Send cell count with differential, Gram stain, aerobic + anaerobic culture, and crystals. Overlying cellulitis is a relative contraindication — prefer an alternative window or image guidance, but do not withhold the tap entirely.DO FIRST
Blood cultures ×2 setsBefore the first antibiotic dose. Positive in roughly a quarter to a half of cases; in Weston's cohort joint and/or blood cultures were positive in 82% combined. Sometimes the blood is the only thing that grows.DO FIRST
CRP + ESRBaseline for trending, which is their real value. Sensitive at low cut-offs (ESR ≥10 mm/h ~97–98%; CRP ≥20 mg/L ~92%) but non-specific. A normal value does not exclude the diagnosis and must not stop you aspirating.Initial
FBC, U&E/creatinine, LFTs, glucose/HbA1cLeukocytosis in only ~50–60%. Renal function is needed now because it sets the vancomycin and β-lactam doses. New hyperglycaemia may be the unrecognised diabetes that let this happen.Initial
Serum lactateIf any systemic features. >2 mmol/L with hypotension after fluids defines septic shock and changes the destination from ward to unit.If unwell
Serum urateOnly to inform the crystal question later — and note it is frequently normal or low during an acute gout flare, so it neither confirms gout nor excludes infection. Never use it to avoid tapping.Adjunct
Gonococcal + chlamydial NAATUrethral/cervical plus pharyngeal plus rectal, based on exposure history, in any sexually active patient — regardless of local symptoms. Overall NAAT sensitivity >75%, far better than joint culture (≤50%). Add HIV and syphilis serology.If young / sexually active
Plain radiograph of the jointOrder it, but know its limits. Usually normal early. Its job is to find what would change your plan: fracture, radio-opaque foreign body, soft-tissue gas, chondrocalcinosis, established erosive change, or a prosthesis you did not know about.Initial
UltrasoundTo confirm and quantify an effusion, and above all to guide aspiration — especially the hip, where it is the modality of choice. It cannot distinguish septic from non-septic fluid, and a normal scan does not exclude infection.If deep / difficult joint
MRI with contrastWhen you suspect concurrent osteomyelitis, an abscess, sacroiliac or spinal involvement, or when the joint cannot be assessed clinically. Changes can appear within 24 h of onset. This is the tool that separates reactive marrow oedema from true bone infection — real osteomyelitis oedema is larger and more multifocal.Targeted
CTMandatory for sternoclavicular joint infection — to look for retrosternal and mediastinal extension and chest-wall abscess, which changes the operation and brings in cardiothoracic surgery. Also the practical choice for sacroiliac joints.SC / SI joint
EchocardiogramIf S. aureus bacteraemia, polyarticular disease, injection drug use, a murmur, or a prosthetic valve. Concurrent endocarditis changes duration and the whole management plan.Indicated subsets
AFB / fungal culture, 16S rRNA PCRAdd when the course is chronic (weeks–months), the host is immunocompromised, there is endemic TB exposure, or routine cultures are negative and the patient is not improving. Ask the lab to hold fungal cultures for weeks.If atypical
📊

Synovial fluid — how to actually read it

Read this as a Bayesian dial, not a cut-off. The count moves your probability; it never settles the question. Cases with counts under 25,000 are well described — early presentation, partially treated disease, immunosuppression, gonococcal infection and prosthetic joints all run low.
Synovial testPerformanceHow to interpret it — and what fools it
WBC count>100,000: LR 28
>50,000: LR 7.7
≥25,000: LR 2.9
<25,000: LR 0.32		The most useful single number, and still not decisive. Falsely LOW in: very early presentation, partially treated disease, immunosuppression/neutropenia, gonococcal infection, prosthetic joints (where the diagnostic threshold is a fraction of this), and disseminated TB/fungal disease. Falsely HIGH (i.e. high without infection) in: crystal disease, reactive arthritis, RA flare and Lyme — all of which can exceed 50,000. The 2023 EBJIS/SANJO guideline grades >50,000/µL as "suggestive but not sufficient" and <25,000/µL as "decreases but does not exclude."
PMN differential≥90%: LR 3.4
<90%: LR 0.34		Adds genuinely independent information to the count. A high count with a low PMN fraction should make you think about non-bacterial causes. Lymphocyte predominance points toward TB, Lyme or viral disease.
Gram stainSens 29–65% (GPC), 40–50% (GNR), ~25% (gonococcus)
Spec 97–100%		A positive stain is close to definitive and immediately narrows your empiric choice; a negative stain is close to worthless. Highly operator- and technique-dependent. Prior antibiotics crush the sensitivity (~58% → ~12%).
Culture~70–90%; 82% when combined with blood cultures (Weston)The whole point of tapping first. Prior antibiotics drop yield from ~79% to ~28%. Inoculating fluid into blood-culture bottles improves recovery, especially for Kingella. Negative culture in 10–20% overall.
CrystalsCoexist in ~1.5–5%, up to 21.3% of surgical seriesFinding crystals does not end the investigation. Negatively birefringent needles = monosodium urate (gout); positively birefringent rhomboids = calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD). Both can sit in a frankly infected joint, particularly in older multi-morbid patients.
Synovial D-lactateCut-off ~0.033–0.04 mmol/L: sens 90–92%, spec 83–85%D-lactate is a bacterial stereoisomer that human cells do not make, which is why it outperforms total lactate. Promising as a rapid screen where available; not yet universally offered.
Synovial total lactate≥5 mmol/L: sens 55%, spec 76%Modest. You may hear ">10 mmol/L is highly specific" quoted from an older study (Moss 1981, LR+ ~22) — but the studies underlying that figure often did not state whether they measured D- or L-lactate, so treat it as historical rather than actionable. Use D-lactate if your lab offers it.
Glucose, LDH, proteinNo reliable pooled performanceLow synovial glucose relative to paired serum, high LDH and high protein are classic supportive findings but are non-specific. Do not make or unmake the diagnosis on them.
Serum procalcitoninSens 54%, spec 95%
LR+ 10.97, LR− 0.49		Useful to rule IN, not to rule out. A PCT under 0.5 ng/mL emphatically does not exclude septic arthritis — nearly half of cases have a low value. If you were hoping for a blood test that lets you skip the tap, this is not it.
Serum WBC / ESR / CRPLR+ only 1.3–1.6 (Margaretten)Nearly useless as standalone diagnostics — they barely move the probability. Their value is entirely in trending on treatment, and CRP is the one to trend.
Monosodium urate crystals under polarised light — needle-shaped and negatively birefringent. Seeing this is not permission to stop looking for infection: crystals and sepsis coexist in up to a fifth of surgically treated septic arthritis series. Report the crystals, and still wait for the culture.
Atlas of Medical Foreign Bodies, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file
🖼️

Imaging — what you see, and when it appears

Modality & findingWhen it appears / performanceWhat it means and why you would order it
Plain radiograph
order in everyone		Often normal in the first daysInsensitive for early diagnosis — but it is cheap, fast, and it finds the things that would change your plan: fracture, foreign body, soft-tissue gas, chondrocalcinosis, an unsuspected prosthesis. It also establishes the baseline you will compare against later.
· Soft-tissue swelling, capsular distension, loss of fat planesEarliest — first few daysNon-specific oedema and effusion. The first thing to change on film.
· Periarticular osteopenia~1–2 weeksHyperaemia-driven regional bone loss. Confirms a genuinely inflammatory process.
· Joint space narrowingDays to weeks — a LATE findingThis is cartilage that has already been destroyed. If you are seeing it, you are behind. It is a marker of delayed diagnosis, not a diagnostic tool.
· Erosions, subchondral destruction, ankylosisWeeks onwardEstablished damage. Predicts secondary osteoarthritis and functional loss.
UltrasoundImmediateExcellent at detecting and quantifying effusion, and the practical tool for guiding aspiration — the modality of choice for the hip. Critically: it cannot tell septic from non-septic fluid. A normal scan does not exclude infection; a large effusion does not confirm it. It tells you where the needle goes, not what the answer is.
MRI (ideally with contrast)Changes within ~24 h of onset
One study: sens 100%, spec 77%		The most sensitive modality. Synovial enhancement, perisynovial oedema, effusion, and — the key question — bone marrow signal change. Distinguishing reactive marrow oedema from true concurrent osteomyelitis matters because osteomyelitis extends the antibiotic course to around 6 weeks. Real bone infection tends to show larger, more multifocal marrow change.
CTImmediateMandatory in sternoclavicular joint infection — mediastinal and retrosternal extension is common enough to change the operation, and this is the classic injection-drug-use presentation. Also the workhorse for sacroiliac joints and for guiding deep aspiration.
Nuclear medicine
bone scan, labelled WBC		Adjunct onlyOccasionally useful when MRI is contraindicated or around existing hardware where MRI is degraded. Not first-line, and too non-specific to drive acute decisions.
Radiographic septic arthritis of the hip. The hip is deep, clinically unassessable, and the one joint where the femoral head's blood supply runs inside the capsule — so a tense septic effusion can infarct it. Image-guided aspiration and same-day theatre. Note that by the time bony change is visible on plain film, cartilage has already been lost.
Fernando Ruiz Santiago et al. (Radiology Research and Practice), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file
Ultrasound of the knee showing joint fluid. Use ultrasound to find the effusion and guide the needle — never to decide whether the fluid is infected. Septic and non-septic effusions look the same.
Nevit Dilmen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file
MRI of a knee with a joint effusion — this particular case is a post-traumatic haemarthrosis, not an infection, and it is included to show how an effusion and the surrounding structures appear on MRI. That ambiguity is the point: MRI is exquisitely sensitive for fluid and soft-tissue change but cannot call it infected on its own. What MRI uniquely answers is the question that changes your antibiotic duration — is the adjacent bone marrow involved too?
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file
🧭

The diagnostic algorithm

The path from hot swollen joint to a decision. Note the two branch points people get wrong: recognising a prosthetic joint before anyone puts a needle in it, and understanding that an indeterminate or low cell count sends you to clinical judgement — not to discharge.
🔀

Differential diagnosis — with the discriminators

ConditionTypical synovial WBCWhat actually discriminates it
Septic arthritisOften >50,000; frequently >100,000; PMN >90%Positive Gram stain or culture, systemic toxicity, monoarticular in ~90%. But remember the overlap below is real and substantial.
Gout / CPPD10,000–70,000 (range 1,000–100,000)Crystals on polarised microscopy — but crystals do not exclude infection. Prior identical attacks, classic first MTP or knee involvement, chondrocalcinosis on film. Serum urate is unreliable acutely.
Reactive arthritis10,000–40,000, PMN-predominantCell counts overlap so much with septic arthritis that the count cannot separate them. You need the history: preceding GI or GU infection 1–4 weeks earlier, conjunctivitis, enthesitis, HLA-B27 — plus a negative culture.
RA flare5,000–50,000, PMN ~60–80%Known RA, symmetric polyarticular pattern, chronicity, response to their usual therapy. But RA is the single biggest risk factor for true septic arthritis — a single hot joint in an RA patient is aspirated, not assumed.
Lyme arthritisCan reach ~47,000–64,000 — overlaps heavilyEndemic exposure, large knee effusion often strikingly less painful than the size suggests, weeks-to-months course. Serology (ELISA → immunoblot) and synovial PCR. Essentially never culture-positive. Treated with antibiotics, not washout.
Viral arthritis
parvovirus B19, HBV/HCV, chikungunya, dengue		Lower-grade, non-purulentSymmetric small-joint polyarthralgia, viral prodrome, rash, travel history. Specific serologies.
Acute rheumatic feverInflammatory, non-purulentMigratory polyarthritis, preceding streptococcal pharyngitis, carditis, raised ASOT — Jones criteria.
Haemarthrosis / trauma / fractureBloody, low WBCTrauma history, anticoagulants or a bleeding disorder. Frank blood on aspiration. Radiograph for fracture. Note trauma and infection can coexist after penetrating injury.
OsteonecrosisNon-inflammatory or mildSteroids, alcohol, sickle cell. MRI is diagnostic. Subacute onset.
Transient synovitis (children)Usually <15,000, almost always <50,000Well-appearing child, afebrile or low-grade fever, normal or mildly raised markers, recent viral illness, and a low Kocher score. This is the diagnosis the Kocher criteria were built to separate from septic hip.
Charcot neuroarthropathyNon-inflammatory or mildThe great mimic in the diabetic foot and ankle: a hot, red, swollen, relatively painless joint in a patient with dense neuropathy. Raised markers and dramatic radiographic destruction make it look infected. Elevating the limb for 5–10 minutes classically settles the erythema in Charcot but not in infection. When you genuinely cannot tell — and often you cannot — aspirate and image, because Charcot and infection coexist in exactly this population.
PVNS / tumourNon-inflammatory, often haemorrhagicChronic recurrent haemarthrosis; characteristic MRI (haemosiderin blooming in PVNS). Biopsy.
Charcot neuroarthropathy on clinical examination. A hot, swollen, deformed but often surprisingly painless joint in a neuropathic patient. This is the differential you are most likely to get wrong in a diabetic foot — and the one where getting it wrong in either direction is costly.
J. Terrence Jose Jerome, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons · source file

Calculators

🧮

Synovial fluid interpreter — Margaretten LRs applied to your pretest probability

This is not a score; it is Bayes' theorem with the published likelihood ratios from Margaretten et al., JAMA 2007. Enter your own clinical pretest probability and the fluid results, and it returns the post-test probability. The point is to make visible how little a "reassuring" cell count actually helps.

Your clinical pretest probability (%)
Rough anchors: a hot joint in a young healthy adult ≈ 10–20%; an acutely hot joint in an RA patient on a biologic, or in an elderly diabetic ≈ 40–60%; frank pus with rigors ≈ 80%+.
Synovial WBC (cells/mm³)
< 25,000 LR 0.32
25,000 – 50,000 LR 2.9
50,000 – 100,000 LR 7.7
> 100,000 LR 28
Synovial PMN fraction
≥ 90% PMN LR 3.4

Not available —
Post-test probability of septic arthritis
—
Watch what happens when you enter a 50% pretest probability with a cell count under 25,000 and PMN under 90% — the two most "reassuring" fluid results available. The post-test probability is still about 10%, which is nowhere near low enough to send someone home on. Margaretten's own conclusion is that no cut-off excludes the diagnosis. A "reassuring" tap in a patient you were genuinely worried about is a reason to keep watching them, repeat the aspirate if they worsen, and treat if the clinical picture demands it — not a discharge letter.
🧸

Kocher criteria — septic arthritis vs transient synovitis of the paediatric hip

Derived by Kocher et al., JBJS 1999 (retrospective, 282 children) and prospectively validated by the same group in 2004 (51 septic arthritis vs 103 transient synovitis). Both probability sets are shown, because the gap between them is the teaching point.

History of fever > 38.5 °C +1
Non-weight-bearing on the affected side +1
ESR > 40 mm/h +1
Serum WBC > 12,000 /mm³ +1
0
predictors present
At 4/4 predictors the derivation cohort said 99.6% and the validation cohort said 93%. At 0/4 the derivation said <0.2% and the validation said 2%. The rule degraded substantially outside its derivation population — a general lesson about prediction rules, and a specific warning here because Kingella kingae (the leading pathogen in children under 4) often produces an indolent illness with a near-normal CRP and no fever, defeating the score entirely. Use Kocher to support the decision to aspirate. Never use it to avoid aspirating.
ModificationThe Caird modification (2006) adds CRP as a fifth variable, reaching ~97.5% probability with all five present. It is not more widely validated than the original, and the same caution applies.
🔗

Related scores — open on a validated calculator

These involve continuous nomograms or point systems better run on a maintained calculator than reproduced from memory:

  • Kocher Criteria (MDCalc) — cross-check the version above
  • SOFA score (MDCalc) — organ dysfunction; SOFA ≥4 performs better than qSOFA for predicting ICU need
  • qSOFA (MDCalc) — bedside sepsis screen; specificity ~87% but sensitivity only ~40%, so it rules in rather than out
  • Charlson Comorbidity Index (MDCalc) — comorbidity burden, which independently predicted outcome in the surgical-delay cohort
  • Cockcroft-Gault CrCl (MDCalc) — you need this before you dose vancomycin or a β-lactam
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

⚖️

How each comorbidity changes the disease AND its management

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes your management
Rheumatoid arthritisOR 4.0; present in ~20% of cases. Blunted presentation — often afebrile with modest markers. Damaged cartilage means faster destruction and worse baseline function to fall back on.Aspirate any single acutely hot joint even without fever. Do not attribute to a flare. Hold the biologic and methotrexate during active infection; involve rheumatology about restarting — there is no validated "resume at week X" figure, so this is a co-management decision, and continuing vs stopping biologics after treated infection is associated with fewer flares in general (non-septic-arthritis-specific) data.
Diabetes mellitusOR 3.3, and an independent predictor of morbidity in Weston 1999. More gram-negative and polymicrobial disease. Neuropathy delays presentation.Broaden empiric gram-negative cover. Examine the feet — a diabetic foot ulcer is both the portal and a reason to image for osteomyelitis. Expect glycaemic control to deteriorate on infection and steroids; use insulin, not oral agents, acutely.
Chronic kidney disease / dialysisCatheter-related bacteraemia is a recurrent seeding source. Metastatic infection from catheter bacteraemia warrants longer therapy.This is where dosing errors happen. Vancomycin needs AUC-guided dosing with pharmacy input; avoid nephrotoxin stacking (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam raises AKI risk — consider cefepime instead). Dose-adjust β-lactams and fluoroquinolones. Remove or exchange the offending catheter — treating the joint while leaving an infected line guarantees relapse.
CirrhosisImpaired opsonisation and complement; higher gram-negative burden; coagulopathy complicates surgery.Broader gram-negative cover. Avoid nephrotoxins given hepatorenal risk. Correct coagulopathy before arthrotomy. Higher mortality — escalate earlier.
Injection drug useUnusual joints (sternoclavicular, sacroiliac, symphysis pubis). Pseudomonas, Serratia, Candida, polymicrobial. Frequently concurrent endocarditis.Ceftriaxone is not enough — you need antipseudomonal cover. Get an echocardiogram. Get a CT if the sternoclavicular joint is involved. Plan the IV access realistically: a PICC may not be safe or feasible, which pushes you toward highly bioavailable oral agents earlier. Offer opioid agonist therapy and harm-reduction support — it materially affects whether they complete treatment.
HIV / transplant / chemotherapy / neutropeniaBlunted systemic signs and lower synovial cell counts. Atypical and opportunistic organisms — mycobacteria, fungi, Nocardia.Broaden cover, send AFB and fungal cultures up front, and lower your threshold for synovial biopsy rather than aspiration alone. A low cell count in this group is expected, not reassuring.
Sickle cell diseaseSalmonella and encapsulated organisms; bone infarction creates the nidus. Functional asplenia.The hard question is always vaso-occlusive crisis or infection — and it is answered with a needle, not with observation. Ensure ceftriaxone or fluoroquinolone cover for Salmonella. Check vaccination status.
Gout / CPPDCoexists in up to 21% of surgical series. Recurrent effusions and damaged cartilage raise risk.Do not let crystals close the case. If you treat the flare, colchicine and NSAIDs are compatible with treating infection, but hold off on steroids until infection is excluded or controlled.
Heart failureLimits fluid resuscitation; congestion is easily worsened by high-sodium antibiotic loads.Remember the sodium content of high-dose penicillins and piperacillin-tazobactam. Resuscitate with attention to volume status; consider the ICU earlier if you cannot fluid-resuscitate safely.
Anticoagulation / bleeding disorderHaemarthrosis mimics and coexists. Surgery is riskier.Therapeutic anticoagulation is not a contraindication to arthrocentesis of an accessible joint — the diagnostic imperative wins. Do involve haematology before arthrotomy and plan reversal.
Avoid or use with real caution: intra-articular corticosteroid (contraindicated in active infection); intra-articular antibiotics (chemical synovitis, no benefit); systemic corticosteroids in adults as routine adjuncts (paediatric RCT evidence exists — Odio 2003, Harel 2011 — but adult evidence is sparse and this should not be reflex practice); rifampin monotherapy (resistance within days — and irrelevant in a native joint anyway); vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam together in anyone with renal risk (additive AKI signal — cefepime is the usual substitute); fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines in pregnancy; prolonged joint immobilisation (drives ankylosis and stiffness, which is the commonest long-term sequela); and NSAIDs in the volume-depleted or renally impaired patient while you are also giving vancomycin.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B screening relevant to this population

GradeRecommendationPopulationWhy it matters here
BChlamydia and gonorrhoea screeningSexually active women ≤24 years, and women ≥25 at increased risk (2021 reaffirmation; evidence in men is an I statement)Disseminated gonococcal infection is the leading cause of septic arthritis in young sexually active adults. Screening prevents the disease upstream — and a septic joint is itself an indication to screen and to treat partners.
AHIV screeningAdolescents and adults 15–65 years; all pregnant persons, each pregnancyImmunosuppression changes both the organism spectrum and the presentation (blunted fever, lower cell counts). DGI and HIV share risk factors — diagnose one, screen for the other.
BHepatitis C screeningAll adults 18–79 yearsHigh yield in people who inject drugs — the population with sternoclavicular and sacroiliac disease and Pseudomonas. Cirrhosis also worsens septic arthritis outcomes.
BHepatitis B screeningAdolescents and adults at increased risk (risk-based, not universal)Same population overlap; also relevant before immunosuppressive therapy in the RA patients who are over-represented here.
BPrediabetes and type 2 diabetes screeningAdults 35–70 years with overweight or obesityDiabetes carries OR 3.3 for septic arthritis and is an independent predictor of permanent joint dysfunction. Finding it early is genuine prevention.
BUnhealthy alcohol use — screening and brief counsellingAdolescents and adultsAlcohol misuse and cirrhosis both raise risk and worsen outcome, and impair the ability to complete a multi-week antibiotic course.
BUnhealthy drug use screeningAdultsDirectly identifies the injection-drug-use population. Linking to opioid agonist therapy and sterile-equipment services is the most effective single prevention available for recurrent septic arthritis in this group.
ATobacco cessation counselling and pharmacotherapyAll adultsImpairs wound healing and surgical outcome after arthrotomy or arthroscopy.

USPSTF recommendations are periodically updated — verify the current grade and age bracket at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org before acting on a specific bracket.

Disease-specific prevention

  • Aseptic injection technique. Absolute risk is low (~0.09–0.18% per large-joint steroid injection) but it is non-zero, foreseeable, and it belongs in your consent conversation. Outbreaks have been traced to unsafe practice — single-dose vials, full skin prep, no shortcuts.
  • Never inject a joint with overlying skin infection, and think hard before injecting a joint you may need to interpret later.
  • Treat skin and soft-tissue infection properly. Skin infection is the strongest risk factor identified (OR 27.2). Diabetic foot care, leg ulcer care and eczema control are septic arthritis prevention.
  • Vaccinate — pneumococcal and influenza per schedule, particularly in RA, diabetes, asplenia/sickle cell and the elderly.
  • Screen for latent TB before starting a TNF inhibitor, and counsel those patients that a single hot joint means same-day assessment, not a wait-and-see.
  • Harm reduction for people who inject drugs: opioid agonist therapy, sterile equipment, skin and vein care education, and low-threshold access when something goes wrong.
Monitor

After discharge — the clinic's real job

📈

Follow-up cadence and what to check

WhenWhat to checkWhat would worry you
1–2 weeks
on therapy		CRP trend, joint examination and range of motion, adherence, line site if on OPAT. Drug-specific monitoring: FBC weekly on linezolid (cytopenias, and watch for neuropathy beyond ~2 weeks), CK weekly on daptomycin, renal function and vancomycin levels, LFTs on rifampin.CRP not falling, or rising. Recurrent effusion. New fever. A red or painful line site.
4–6 weeks
end of therapy		CRP should have normalised — it typically does within about a week of effective treatment. Function, range of motion, analgesia needs. Decide with rheumatology about restarting DMARDs or biologics.Persistently raised CRP at the end of the course, or symptoms recurring as you stop. Both mean re-image and re-culture, not another blind course.
3 monthsFunctional recovery, need for physiotherapy, radiographs if there is ongoing pain or a mechanical symptom. Address the risk factor that caused it — glycaemic control, skin care, substance use, immunosuppression plan.New or worsening pain, mechanical symptoms, or joint-space loss on film — the beginning of post-infectious osteoarthritis, which affects roughly a third of patients.
CRP trajectory is the single most useful thing you trend. It normalises within about a week with effective treatment — and a slow fall by post-operative day 3 and day 5 has been specifically associated with treatment failure and the need for further surgery. A CRP that is coming down slowly is an actionable finding, not a number to note and move past.
Warn every patient at discharge about the specific things that mean come back today: fever returning, the joint swelling or becoming hot again, new pain, a new painful joint, or a red/tender IV line. Roughly a third of patients experience treatment failure at one year — and the ones who do best are the ones who present early when it happens.
Escalate

When to send them in

🚑

Red flags → same-day ED

Suspected septic arthritis is itself the red flag. An acutely hot, swollen, painfully restricted joint goes to the ED the same day — with a phone call, not just a letter. Do not wait for the CRP. Do not start oral antibiotics first.
FindingWhy it escalates
Any suspected septic native jointNeeds aspiration, IV antibiotics and a drainage decision within 24 hours. Not deliverable in clinic.
Suspected septic HIP, shoulder, sacroiliac or sternoclavicular jointCannot be aspirated adequately at the bedside; the hip risks avascular necrosis. Needs image-guided aspiration and surgical review the same day.
Any prosthetic joint that becomes acutely painful, hot or starts drainingDo not aspirate it in clinic. Contaminating the tap wrecks the diagnostic pathway. Refer directly to the arthroplasty service.
Two or more involved jointsPolyarticular disease carries several-fold higher mortality and implies ongoing bacteraemia — needs inpatient workup for endocarditis.
Fever with rigors, hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, or lactate >2Sepsis. Confusion at presentation was an independent predictor of death in Weston's cohort. Blue-light transfer, not a routine referral.
Immunocompromised host — biologic, transplant, chemotherapy, neutropeniaPresentation is blunted, so by the time it looks impressive it is advanced. Lower the threshold, not raise it.
A bite over a joint, or any penetrating injury involving a jointAssume joint penetration. Fight-bite injuries over the MCP joints need surgical exploration, not oral antibiotics.
Neurovascular compromise, or skin necrosis / crepitus / pain out of proportionConsider necrotising soft-tissue infection — a separate surgical emergency that can coexist. Immediate surgical referral.
Say the words "I am worried about septic arthritis" in your referral. It is a phrase that reliably gets a joint aspirated. "Query gout, please review" reliably does not.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria — and the honest answer

Admit everyone with suspected or confirmed native joint septic arthritis. Every reviewed guideline defaults to inpatient care; mean UK length of stay is around 11.5 days. Outpatient management appears in the literature essentially only for selected haemodynamically stable paediatric cohorts with strict follow-up. In adults, the question is not whether to admit but to which level of care, and how fast the joint gets drained.
Level of careCriteriaWhat drives the decision
Ward, standardHaemodynamically stable, no organ dysfunction, single accessible joint, lactate ≤2, able to take oral intake, no airway concernMost patients. Needs IV antibiotics, a same-day drainage plan, orthopaedic and ID input.
Ward with higher observation / step-up bedTachycardic or borderline BP responsive to fluids; lactate 2–4; polyarticular; frail elderly; significant comorbidity (CKD, cirrhosis, immunosuppression)These patients declare themselves in the first 24 hours. If you are unsure, put them somewhere with more frequent observations rather than gambling on the floor.
ICUSee the ICU panel — vasopressor requirement, lactate >4, qSOFA ≥2 with organ dysfunction, respiratory failure, GCS dropSeptic shock, or a joint infection that is one component of multi-organ sepsis.
Straight to theatre from EDSeptic hip; septic shoulder, sacroiliac or sternoclavicular joint; loculated or frankly purulent large joint; any concern for necrotising soft-tissue infectionThe bed can be sorted out afterwards. Delay to surgery independently predicts death (HR 1.7 for 1-year mortality) and treatment failure (HR 1.5).
Arthroplasty service, not general medicineAny prosthetic jointDifferent disease, different diagnostic thresholds, different operation. Do not aspirate it on the ward.
The clock that matters is time to source control. The 2023 EBJIS/SANJO guideline states that in a patient who is not septic, surgery "can be postponed but no longer than 24 hours" — and notes this is a weak recommendation from low-quality evidence (Grade D2). In a patient who is septic, it is now. Either way, "we will discuss it at the trauma meeting tomorrow" is not an acceptable plan for a septic joint.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

The first hour, in order

1. Blood cultures ×2Before antibiotics. From two separate sites. If a central line is present, one set from the line and one peripheral.FIRST
2. ArthrocentesisBefore antibiotics if the patient is stable. Cell count + differential, Gram stain, aerobic and anaerobic culture, crystals. Send a portion in blood-culture bottles — it improves recovery, especially for fastidious organisms. Add AFB/fungal and 16S PCR if the course is chronic or the host is immunocompromised.FIRST
3. Empiric IV antibioticsImmediately after the tap — or immediately, without waiting, if the patient is septic or unstable. Weight and creatinine must be on the chart before you dose.FIRST HOUR
4. Orthopaedics referralSame day, every patient. This is a joint decision about drainage, not a courtesy call. State the joint, the fluid appearance, the cell count if back, and whether the patient is septic.FIRST HOUR
FBC, U&E, creatinine, LFT, CRP, ESR, glucose/HbA1c, coagulationOn admission. Creatinine and weight set your antibiotic doses. Coagulation matters if they are going to theatre.Admit
Serum lactateOn admission and repeat at 2–4 h if the first is >2 mmol/L. Failure to clear is an ICU trigger.Admit
Radiograph of the affected jointOn admission — baseline, plus to exclude fracture, foreign body, gas and an unsuspected prosthesis.Admit
MRSA screen (nasal PCR)On admission. A positive nasal screen was far commoner in MRSA arthritis (51%) than MSSA arthritis (5.6%) in one cohort — genuinely useful for refining empiric cover, and useful for de-escalation logic too.Admit
Gonococcal + chlamydial NAAT; HIV, syphilis, HBV, HCV serologyAny sexually active patient, and anyone who injects drugs. All exposed sites for the NAAT.Selected
EchocardiogramS. aureus bacteraemia, polyarticular disease, injection drug use, murmur, prosthetic valve or pacemaker. TTE first; TOE if TTE is negative and suspicion remains.Selected
CT of the joint ± chestMandatory for sternoclavicular joint infection to assess mediastinal and chest-wall extension. Also for sacroiliac joints.SC / SI joint
MRI with contrastIf concurrent osteomyelitis, abscess or spinal involvement is suspected, or the joint is inaccessible to examination. The answer changes your antibiotic duration.Selected
Analgesia — multimodalParacetamol plus an NSAID if renal function and volume status allow (be careful with concurrent vancomycin), plus short-acting opioid for procedures. Under-treated pain is the commonest reason patients refuse the physiotherapy that prevents ankylosis.Admit
VTE prophylaxisAcute infection plus an immobilised limb plus likely surgery. Prescribe per your local medical inpatient protocol, adjusted for renal function and the surgical plan. Note there are no septic-arthritis-specific data — this is standard inpatient practice.Admit
Physiotherapy referralDay 1 — not day 5. Early gentle range of motion or continuous passive motion. Cartilage needs cyclical loading; adhesions form fast. Roughly 39% of patients in the Gjika trial had mechanical sequelae, dominated by stiffness and adhesions.Admit
Hold DMARDs / biologics / non-essential immunosuppressionOn admission, in discussion with rheumatology. Restarting is a co-management decision — there is no validated "resume at week X" figure.If applicable
ID consultSame day for: MRSA, gram-negative or Pseudomonas isolates, culture-negative disease not improving, penicillin allergy, prosthetic joint, endocarditis, or any plan for OPAT.Admit
Sequence matters more than speed here. The one thing you cannot get back is the pre-antibiotic culture. If the patient is stable, the order is cultures → tap → antibiotics. If the patient is septic, antibiotics do not wait — but say so explicitly in the notes so nobody later misreads a negative culture as absence of infection.
Treat

Antibiotics — full dose ladders

💊

Step 1 — empiric therapy, chosen by Gram stain and host

Empiric choice answers two questions: do I need MRSA cover? and do I need gram-negative or antipseudomonal cover? Everything else is detail. Cover S. aureus in everyone.
ScenarioRegimenReasoning
Gram-positive cocci on stain, or no organism seen — MRSA risk present
the usual starting point		Vancomycin (dose ladder below)
+ ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h if the patient is elderly, immunocompromised, diabetic, has a urinary/GI source, or is sexually active		Covers MRSA, MSSA, streptococci and community gram-negatives. This is the default in most US practice. Note the alternative approach in the GEIO-SEIMC/SEIP/SECOT 2023–24 guideline for adults with a negative stain and no resistance risk factors: cloxacillin plus ceftriaxone, or amoxicillin-clavulanate monotherapy — reasonable where MRSA prevalence is low.
Gram-negative bacilli on stainCeftriaxone 2 g IV q24h, or cefepime 2 g IV q8–12h if Pseudomonas is plausibleDo not drop staphylococcal cover until culture confirms, unless the stain is unequivocal.
Gram-negative diplococci, or the DGI storyCeftriaxone 1 g IV/IM q24h + doxycycline 100 mg PO BD × 7 days if chlamydia not excludedCDC 2021. Oral step-down 24–48 h after substantial improvement, guided by susceptibilities (cefixime 800 mg BD if none available); total ≥7 days.
Injection drug useVancomycin + an antipseudomonal β-lactam — cefepime 2 g IV q8h, or piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h, or ceftazidime 2 g IV q8hCeftriaxone does not cover Pseudomonas. This is the single commonest empiric error in this population. Also think Candida and polymicrobial disease, and get an echocardiogram.
Immunocompromised / neutropenic / post-transplantVancomycin + cefepime (or piperacillin-tazobactam / meropenem per local resistance)Broad gram-negative and antipseudomonal cover. Send AFB and fungal cultures up front and lower the threshold for biopsy — the cell count will under-represent the disease.
Animal bite (cat/dog)Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV q6h, or amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BD if not requiring IVPasteurella multocida is resistant to first-generation cephalosporins, clindamycin and flucloxacillin — the reflex "cellulitis" antibiotics all miss it.
Human bite / fight bite over the MCP jointsAmpicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV q6h + hand surgery reviewEikenella corrodens — also resistant to clindamycin and first-generation cephalosporins. These wounds need formal exploration, not antibiotics alone.
Sickle cell diseaseVancomycin + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24hCeftriaxone covers Salmonella as well as pneumococcus. And take the tap — you cannot tell vaso-occlusive crisis from infection clinically.
Chronic monoarthritis over weeks–monthsHold empiric antibacterials if stable; pursue synovial biopsy, AFB and fungal culture, and TB workupYou will not cure TB or Sporothrix with vancomycin, and empiric treatment here just delays the diagnosis.

Vancomycin — the full ladder

StepDoseTitration / monitoringTarget / maxNotes
Loading dose20–35 mg/kg actual body weight IV — commonly 25–30 mg/kg in serious infection or critical illnessGive once, up front. Infuse at ≤10 mg/min (or over ≥60 min) to avoid an infusion reaction.Max 3,000 mg for the loadGets you into the therapeutic range immediately instead of after 24–48 h of subtherapeutic exposure. Use actual body weight, including in obesity. ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP 2020.
Maintenance15–20 mg/kg actual body weight IV q8–12hAdjust interval to renal function (q12h is typical for normal CrCl; extend for CKD; dialysis dosing per pharmacy). Draw levels for AUC-guided dosing — two-level or Bayesian, per your service.AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600 mg·h/L
Max 4,500 mg/day		Binds D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan precursors — upstream of the altered PBP2a that makes MRSA β-lactam resistant. AUC-guided dosing replaced trough-only monitoring in 2020 because it delivers the same efficacy with less nephrotoxicity.
If AUC monitoring is unavailableSame dosesTrough 15–20 mg/L as a surrogate, drawn immediately before the 4th–5th doseTrough 15–20 mg/LExplicitly the inferior option now — trough-only targeting overshoots AUC and drives AKI. Nephrotoxicity risk climbs as daily AUC exceeds roughly 650 mg·h/L.
Monitoring on starting—Creatinine at least every 48 h (daily if unstable, on other nephrotoxins, or in AKI); levels with dose changes and at least weekly; FBC if prolonged—Watch for AKI, and for DRESS — fever, rash, eosinophilia, organ involvement at 2–6 weeks. That is a true severe reaction requiring permanent avoidance.
Unknown prior dose / no recordsDose from current weight and creatinine, not from historyVancomycin is always dosed de novo from renal function — there is no "home dose" to resumeAs aboveUnlike chronic oral therapy, there is nothing to guess at here. Get a weight and a creatinine and calculate.
"Red man syndrome" is a rate-related histamine release, not an allergy. Slow the infusion and pre-medicate with an antihistamine — do not relabel the patient as vancomycin-allergic and switch them to a worse drug for life. A genuine vancomycin allergy is DRESS or another severe cutaneous adverse reaction.
Avoid pairing vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam where there is any renal risk — the combination carries a consistent additive AKI signal. Cefepime is the usual substitute when you need antipseudomonal cover alongside vancomycin.
🎯

Step 2 — narrow to the organism (all the real options in each class)

The moment susceptibilities are back, de-escalate. This is not just stewardship — for MSSA specifically, a β-lactam outperforms vancomycin, so staying on vancomycin because it is "already running" actively disadvantages the patient.

MSSA — pick a β-lactam, and know why you would pick each

DrugStartTitration / adjustmentTarget / maxWhy it worksIf allergic / intolerant
Cefazolin
usual default		2 g IV q8hReduce interval extension only for renal impairment (q12h for CrCl 11–34; consult pharmacy below that). 3 g q8h is used in obesity at some centres.6 g/day typical; up to 12 g/day describedInhibits PBP-mediated transpeptidation → bactericidal cell-wall failure. Better tolerated than nafcillin/oxacillin — less phlebitis, less hepatotoxicity, less interstitial nephritis, and q8h rather than q4h dosing makes OPAT far more practical.Safe in most non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy (cross-reactivity <2% with dissimilar side chains). In true anaphylaxis: vancomycin, daptomycin or linezolid.
Nafcillin2 g IV q4hNo renal adjustment needed (hepatically cleared) — an advantage in renal failure. Monitor LFTs and watch the IV site closely.12 g/daySame PBP mechanism, and not susceptible to the cefazolin inoculum effect.Significant phlebitis (needs a good line), hepatotoxicity, and interstitial nephritis. q4h dosing is impractical for outpatient therapy.
Oxacillin2 g IV q4hAs nafcillin. Monitor LFTs.12 g/dayEquivalent to nafcillin; choice is usually institutional habit and supply.Same tolerability problems as nafcillin.
Flucloxacillin
UK / Europe / Australia		2 g IV q6h (BSR 2006 empiric guidance was 1 g QDS; 2 g q6h is common current practice for deep infection)Monitor LFTs — cholestatic hepatitis risk rises with age and duration.8–12 g/dayThe antistaphylococcal penicillin of choice outside North America; same PBP target.Cholestatic jaundice, especially over age 55 and beyond 2 weeks. Not active against Pasteurella or Eikenella.
The cefazolin "inoculum effect." Some MSSA strains produce a type A β-lactamase that hydrolyses cefazolin — but not oxacillin or nafcillin — at high bacterial density, raising the effective MIC. It affects perhaps 10–30% of strains in vitro, but clinical outcome comparisons are largely reassuring once source control is achieved. A defensible practical approach: oxacillin or nafcillin while the burden is high and undrained (persistent bacteraemia, no source control yet), then switch to cefazolin once the joint is drained and blood cultures have cleared — you get the tolerability and the convenient dosing when it is safe to have them.
