Penicillin and cephalosporin allergy — a practical pathway

Reported reactionWhat it actually meansWhat to give
"Rash as a child," no detailThe overwhelming majority are not IgE-mediated, and most are not reproducible on challenge.Cephalosporins are fine — cross-reactivity with a dissimilar side chain is <2%. Use cefazolin for MSSA. Refer for formal allergy assessment; delabelling meaningfully improves the antibiotics this patient gets for the rest of their life.
Delayed benign maculopapular rashT-cell mediated, not anaphylaxis.Cephalosporin with a dissimilar side chain is generally well tolerated.
True anaphylaxis, urticaria within an hour, angioedema, bronchospasmIgE-mediated. Avoid all penicillins.Vancomycin, daptomycin or linezolid for gram-positives; aztreonam (no meaningful β-lactam cross-reactivity) or a fluoroquinolone for gram-negatives. Involve ID.
SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, drug-induced haemolysis or interstitial nephritisSevere non-IgE reaction.Avoid the whole class permanently. No challenge, no test dose. Non-β-lactam therapy, ID-directed.
Cephalosporin allergy with gonococcal arthritisThe hard corner.CDC is explicit that no alternative agent reliably treats DGI. This requires ID consultation — and depending on the situation, desensitisation.
🔄

Step 3 — IV to oral, and how long in total

This is genuinely unsettled, and you should know that rather than quote a single number. Two good bodies of evidence point in different directions, and the reconciling variable is adequacy of source control and which joint.
SourceWhat it saysHow to use it
EBJIS/SANJO 2023
the most current graded international guideline		IV 1–2 weeks, then oral 2–4 weeks — roughly 3–4 weeks total for typical adult native joint disease (Grade D2). For ACL-reconstruction-associated infection: 1–2 weeks IV then 4–5 weeks oral.A sensible default framework. Note the grade — D2 means weak recommendation from low-quality evidence, which is an honest reflection of the field.
Gjika 2019 (ARD)
the only directly applicable RCT		154 adults randomised after surgical drainage: 2 weeks non-inferior to 4 weeks (cure 76/77 vs 75/77; recurrence 1 vs 2, p=0.58). Median IV duration was only 1–2 days. Hospital stay 4 vs 6 days.Read the population carefully: 64% were hand and wrist joints, and the authors themselves frame the conclusion as holding "at least for hand and wrist arthritis." Also note substantial sequelae in both arms (39% overall) — and the sequelae endpoint did not meet non-inferiority.
Korean cohort 2023
the countervailing data		137 culture-positive native joint cases, mostly large joints: antibiotics ≤4 weeks was associated with relapse — OR 25.47 (95% CI 1.57–412.33). Overall relapse 9.5%. Synovial WBC ≥150,000 also predicted relapse (OR 17.46).The wide confidence interval reflects small numbers, but the direction is consistent and the population is the one you usually have on the ward. Do not apply Gjika's 2 weeks to a large joint.
OVIVA 2019 (NEJM)1,054 patients with complex bone and joint infection: oral non-inferior to IV for the first 6 weeks (risk difference −1.38%, 90% CI −4.94 to +2.19). Catheter complications 0.96% oral vs 9.37% IV.Practice-changing for the route, and it demolishes the "bone and joint infection needs 6 weeks of IV" dogma. But the population was overwhelmingly osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint and diabetic foot infection — not native joint septic arthritis. Use it to justify early oral switch with a bioavailable drug; do not cite it as septic-arthritis-specific.

A defensible practical framework

SituationIV phaseTotal duration
Small joint (hand, wrist, foot), adequately drained, susceptible organism, good clinical and CRP responseUntil clearly improving — often only a few days2–3 weeks (Gjika applies most directly here)
Large joint (knee, shoulder, ankle, elbow), adequately drained, uncomplicated1–2 weeks3–4 weeks (EBJIS/SANJO framework)
S. aureus, especially MRSA; or bacteraemic≥2 weeks, and count from the first negative blood culture4 weeks or more; if endocarditis, follow the endocarditis duration instead
Concurrent osteomyelitis1–2 weeks~6 weeks
Hip; or inadequate/delayed source control; or immunocompromised; or slow CRP fallLonger, individualised≥4–6 weeks, ID-directed
GonococcalCeftriaxone until 24–48 h of substantial improvement≥7 days total (CDC 2021)
Prosthetic jointPer the arthroplasty/ID pathwayMuch longer — staphylococcal DAIR: ~3 months hip, ~6 months knee with rifampin (IDSA 2013); non-staphylococcal DAIR 4–6 weeks. Never extrapolate native-joint short courses here.

Requirements before you switch to oral

  • Source control achieved — the joint has been drained adequately and is not reaccumulating.
  • Clinically improving — afebrile, pain and swelling settling, function returning.
  • CRP falling convincingly. A slow fall at post-operative day 3 and day 5 is specifically associated with treatment failure and the need for further surgery — that is a reason to delay the switch and re-examine the joint, not to proceed.
  • Blood cultures negative if they were ever positive.
  • A susceptible, highly bioavailable oral agent exists — linezolid, a fluoroquinolone, clindamycin, TMP-SMX, doxycycline, or an oral β-lactam for streptococci.
  • The patient will actually take it — adherence, no malabsorption, no vomiting, and a realistic plan if they inject drugs or are unhoused.
Rifampin is for hardware, not for native joints. Its role is biofilm on retained prosthetic material, added only after debridement and after a companion agent is established — never as monotherapy, because resistance emerges within days. Adding it reflexively to a native joint infection buys you a potent CYP450 inducer (wrecking warfarin, DOACs, oral contraceptives, statins, tacrolimus, HIV protease inhibitors and methadone), hepatotoxicity, and orange body fluids, for no benefit.
Source control

Drainage — the decision that saves the joint

🔧

Which drainage, and when to change your mind

The source-control pathway. The two decisions that matter most: recognising the joints that must go to theatre regardless, and recognising when serial aspiration has failed rather than continuing it out of momentum.
ModalityBest forEvidence & caveats
Serial needle aspiration
daily, to dryness		Accessible joints — above all the knee — in a patient who is responding, with no loculation, no adjacent osteomyelitis, no foreign bodyReasonable first-line for the knee. Ravindran (Rheumatology 2009) compared 32 aspiration vs 19 surgical cases with no baseline comorbidity difference between groups — one of the few direct comparisons, and it does not settle the question. Requires genuine daily commitment: an aspiration plan that quietly lapses after day 2 is worse than an operation.
Arthroscopic lavage
increasingly first-line surgical option		Most large joints; allows visualisation, breakdown of loculations, thorough washout, and a drainMeta-analysis found comparable eradication rates to open arthrotomy with less morbidity. One series: full recovery in 93%, though 25% needed more than one lavage. Host status dominates — compromised "Type C" hosts had >16× the risk of failure after a single lavage compared with healthy hosts.
Open arthrotomyDelayed presentation, thick loculated pus, concurrent osteomyelitis or abscess, technically inaccessible joints, failure of less invasive drainageWeston 1999 found open drainage independently associated with worse morbidity — but this is almost certainly confounding by indication (the worst joints were the ones opened), not a causal harm of arthrotomy. Do not let that finding talk you out of an operation the joint needs.

Joints that essentially always go to theatre

JointWhy
Hip — absoluteThe femoral head's blood supply runs inside the capsule. Intracapsular pressure causes avascular necrosis. Needle aspiration is not definitive management, and imaging-guided aspiration is a diagnostic step on the way to theatre, not an alternative to it. Same day.
ShoulderDeep, difficult to drain adequately percutaneously. Some evidence favours open arthrotomy over arthroscopy specifically here.
SternoclavicularCannot be reliably aspirated. Extends to the retrosternal space, mediastinum and chest wall. Get the CT first, and involve cardiothoracic surgery. Frequently does not respond to antibiotics alone.
SacroiliacDeep and not conventionally aspirable; needs CT or MRI and image-guided or surgical drainage.
Any prosthetic jointBiofilm. Requires the DAIR-versus-exchange algorithm, not lavage.
When has needle drainage failed? There is no single validated "day X" threshold — the literature does not provide one, and you should not pretend otherwise. Escalate to theatre when you see any of: purulent effusion that keeps reaccumulating; persistently positive cultures on repeat aspiration; synovial WBC that fails to fall across 2–3 sequential taps; ongoing fever or systemic signs; or no clinical improvement after several days of adequate antibiotics plus daily aspiration. Note that the EBJIS 24-hour figure applies to initial surgical timing, not to this escalation decision.
Start physiotherapy on day 1. Cartilage is nourished by cyclical loading and diffusion, and denuded surfaces adhere to each other quickly. Around 39% of Gjika's patients had mechanical or neurological sequelae — stiffness, adhesions and flexion loss dominated. The joint needs rest from weight-bearing, not immobility. Continuous passive motion or gentle assisted range of motion from the outset is part of the treatment, not rehabilitation afterwards.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend every day, and what each trend means

WhatFrequencyExpected trajectoryWhat a bad trend means
CRPDaily initially, then alternate daysFalls steadily; normalises within roughly 1 week of effective treatmentA slow fall at post-operative day 3 and day 5 is specifically associated with treatment failure and the need for further surgery. This is the single most actionable number on the chart. A plateau or rise means undrained pus, an abscess, osteomyelitis, the wrong organism, or a resistant organism — re-examine, re-image, re-culture.
Temperature and observationsEvery 4–6 hDefervescence within 48–72 hPersistent fever beyond 72 h of adequate therapy plus drainage = look for undrained collection, a second joint, endocarditis, line infection or drug fever.
Joint examinationDaily, by someone who examined it yesterdayLess pain, less warmth, less effusion, improving passive rangeA tense, reaccumulating effusion is the earliest sign that drainage is inadequate. This is a clinical finding, not a laboratory one — which is why it must be examined and documented daily.
Repeat aspiration ± synovial WBCDaily if managing with serial aspiration; otherwise if not improvingFalling cell count, culture becoming sterileA cell count that does not fall across 2–3 taps is failure of needle drainage → theatre.
Blood culturesRepeat until negative if initially positiveClear within 48–72 hPersistent S. aureus bacteraemia beyond 72 h mandates a hunt for another focus — echocardiogram, spine imaging, line removal — and extends duration substantially.
Creatinine and electrolytesAt least every 48 h; daily if unstable or on vancomycin plus another nephrotoxinStableRising creatinine on vancomycin → recheck AUC, review nephrotoxin stacking, consider daptomycin or linezolid instead.
Drug-specific monitoringWeekly minimum—Vancomycin: levels, creatinine. Daptomycin: CK. Linezolid: FBC (platelets), and neuropathy/vision beyond 2 weeks. TMP-SMX: potassium, creatinine, FBC. Rifampin (hardware only): LFTs. β-lactams: FBC, LFTs on prolonged courses.
GlucosePer diabetes statusControlledInfection and any steroid exposure will worsen control; poor control impairs neutrophil function and healing. Use insulin acutely.
Function and physiotherapy progressDailySteadily increasing range of motionFailure to progress predicts the stiffness and adhesions that are the commonest long-term sequela. Escalate physiotherapy input and analgesia rather than accepting it.
Ask one question on every ward round: "Is this joint better than it was yesterday?" If the answer is no on day 3, something is undrained, something is wrong with the antibiotic, or the diagnosis is wrong. Those are the only three options, and each has a specific next step — re-image, re-culture, or reconsider.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Numeric escalation triggers

These are the standard Sepsis-3 thresholds — there is no septic-arthritis-specific ICU trigger set in the literature, and it would be dishonest to invent one. What is specific to this disease is that the source is drainable, so any escalation conversation must include "has this joint actually been drained yet?"
TriggerThresholdAction
Septic shockVasopressor needed to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg plus lactate >2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitationICU now. Central access, arterial line, norepinephrine. And get the joint drained — this is a source-control problem.
Lactate>4 mmol/L, or failure to clear on repeat at 2–4 hICU referral. Rising lactate despite fluids and antibiotics usually means undrained source.
qSOFA≥2 of: SBP ≤100, RR ≥22, altered mentation (GCS <15)Escalate assessment. Note qSOFA specificity ~87% but sensitivity only ~40% — it rules in, not out. A qSOFA of 0 in a patient you are worried about means nothing.
SOFA≥4Better single predictor of ICU need (sens ~83%, spec ~72%, AUROC 0.81). Use it when qSOFA is equivocal.
Blood pressureSBP <90 or MAP <65 after 30 mL/kg crystalloidVasopressors — which means ICU.
RespiratoryRR >30, SpO₂ <90% on ≥6 L, rising FiO₂ requirement, PaO₂/FiO₂ <300ICU. Consider concurrent pneumonia, septic pulmonary emboli (think right-sided endocarditis in IVDU), or ARDS.
NeurologicalNew confusion or GCS drop ≥2ICU assessment. Confusion at presentation was an independent predictor of death in Weston's cohort — treat it as an organ failure, not as "being a bit muddled."
RenalOliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h, creatinine rise ≥2× baseline, or refractory hyperkalaemia/acidosisICU/renal for possible RRT. Review every nephrotoxin on the chart.
HaematologicalPlatelets <100 falling, INR >1.5, or DICICU. Also delays surgery — involve haematology early so the operation is not postponed twice.
Disease-specificPolyarticular sepsis; necrotising soft-tissue infection suspected; sternoclavicular infection with mediastinal extension; concurrent endocarditisThese need ICU-level monitoring and often urgent multi-team surgery regardless of the current vital signs.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness criteria, and where they go

Discharge readiness — all of these

  • Afebrile ≥24–48 h and haemodynamically stable off any support.
  • Source control complete — the joint has been adequately drained and is not reaccumulating on examination.
  • CRP falling convincingly — not merely "not rising." A plateau is a reason to stay.
  • Blood cultures negative if they were ever positive.
  • Definitive antibiotic plan in place — organism, agent, dose, route, stop date, and who owns the decision to stop.
  • Either a working oral regimen, or a functioning OPAT pathway with the line, the district nursing and the monitoring bloods arranged.
  • Mobilising safely with physiotherapy assessment and equipment in place, and adequate oral analgesia.
  • Follow-up booked — orthopaedics and ID/rheumatology at 1–2 weeks, then 4–6 weeks, then 3 months.
  • The patient can say what would make them come back — recurrent fever, joint swelling or heat, new pain, a new joint, or a red line site.
Not yet ready if: the CRP is plateaued or rising; the joint still reaccumulates; blood cultures are still positive; a planned second washout has not happened; there is no viable route for the remaining antibiotic course; the patient cannot mobilise safely; or nobody has decided who is stopping the antibiotics and when. Roughly a third of patients experience treatment failure within a year — discharging into an unfinished plan is how that happens.

OPAT eligibility (IDSA 2018 framework)

  • ≥5 further days of IV therapy planned — otherwise finish it inpatient or switch to oral.
  • Stable, appropriate venous access and someone competent to care for it.
  • A safe home environment — running water, a telephone, refrigeration for the drug.
  • Patient or carer able to administer, or nursing arranged, and able to give informed consent.
  • Weekly monitoring bloods booked, with a named clinician reviewing them.
  • Rapid access back in if something goes wrong.
Ceftriaxone 2 g once daily is the OPAT-friendly workhorse for susceptible streptococci and Enterobacterales. For MSSA, cefazolin q8h is far more OPAT-practical than nafcillin q4h. And where a bioavailable oral agent will do the job — linezolid, a fluoroquinolone, clindamycin, TMP-SMX — OVIVA says use it and skip the line entirely: catheter complications were 9.37% with IV versus 0.96% with oral.
Think carefully before placing a PICC in someone who actively injects drugs — a central line can be used for injecting, with catastrophic consequences. This is precisely the situation where a highly bioavailable oral regimen, supported by opioid agonist therapy and genuine engagement, is safer than the "gold standard" IV course.

Home

Independent, oral regimen or self-administered OPAT, safe environment, reliable follow-up. The goal for most patients.

Home + home health

Needs district nursing for IV administration, line care, or wound care. Also for physiotherapy in the home when mobility is limited but stable.

SNF

Needs 24-hour skilled nursing plus IV therapy, but less than ~3 h of therapy per day. Common for frail elderly patients after a hip or knee washout.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines with genuine rehabilitation potential — typically after significant functional loss from a large-joint infection or prolonged ICU stay.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care >25 days — ventilator weaning, multiple washouts, complex wounds, or extended IV therapy in a medically fragile patient.

Hospice / palliative

Consider genuinely in the frail elderly patient with polyarticular sepsis and multi-organ failure. Mortality in the over-80s has been reported as high as 22–69%; comfort-focused care with antibiotics as symptom control is a legitimate and sometimes kinder plan.
🫀 ICU — critical care & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When a septic joint belongs in the unit

Only about 5–10% of septic arthritis presents with shock, because the bacterial burden is compartmentalised inside a capsule. When it does, ask immediately why the compartment failed to contain it — and the answer is almost always one of a short list.

Why is this patient shocked?What to look forWhat it changes
1. A large undrained jointTense effusion, a joint that was "planned for tomorrow's list," a hip that was aspirated but never openedThis is the commonest reversible cause and the one you control. Source control is resuscitation. A shocked patient with an undrained septic joint goes to theatre on vasopressors — you do not wait to optimise them first.
2. Concurrent infective endocarditisS. aureus bacteraemia, polyarticular disease, injection drug use, new murmur, prosthetic valve, septic pulmonary emboli on CTEchocardiogram — TTE then TOE. Changes duration entirely, brings in cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, and often explains why the patient is not responding.
3. Necrotising soft-tissue infectionPain out of proportion, skin necrosis or bullae, crepitus, rapidly advancing erythema, very high CRP and lactate, Group A streptococcusA separate surgical emergency that can coexist. Immediate surgical exploration — imaging must not delay it. Add clindamycin or linezolid for toxin suppression and consider IVIG per local practice.
4. Polyarticular diseaseTwo or more joints, immunocompromised or RA hostMortality several-fold higher than monoarticular — reported figures of 32%, 40% in RA specifically, and up to 50% versus around 11% for single-joint disease. Every joint needs a drainage plan.
5. Sternoclavicular joint with mediastinal extensionIVDU, chest or shoulder-girdle pain, retrosternal tendernessCT chest. Mediastinitis or chest-wall abscess needs cardiothoracic surgery, not a bedside aspiration.
6. The frail elderly hostAge >80, confusion, minimal fever, multiple comorbiditiesReported 90-day mortality in this group ranges from 22% to 69%. Escalate early and have the goals-of-care conversation early — both, not one instead of the other.
Formal ICU criteriaThreshold
Septic shock (Sepsis-3)Vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation
Lactate>4 mmol/L, or failure to clear on repeat
SOFA≥4 (sens ~83%, spec ~72%, AUROC 0.81 for predicting ICU need)
qSOFA≥2 — but note sensitivity is only ~40%. Use it to rule in; never to rule out.
Respiratory failureRequiring NIV or intubation; PaO₂/FiO₂ <300; rising FiO₂ requirement
AKI requiring RRTRefractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, oliguria or uraemia
Need for theatre while unstableAny patient going for washout on vasopressors, or requiring repeated urgent washouts
Source control is not a competing priority with resuscitation — it is part of it. Delay to surgery independently predicted 1-year mortality (HR 1.7, 95% CI 1.1–2.6) and treatment failure (HR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1–2.0) after adjusting for age and comorbidity. "Too unstable for theatre" is very rarely true for a joint washout, and it is frequently the reason a patient stays unstable.
Resuscitate

The first 6 hours

💧

Sepsis bundle, applied to this disease

ElementTargetThe septic-arthritis-specific point
Cultures before antibiotics2 sets blood + joint aspirateIn the shocked patient, antibiotics do not wait — but a joint aspirate takes two minutes and can be done in parallel with resuscitation. Get it if you possibly can, and document clearly if you could not.
Broad-spectrum antibioticsWithin 1 hourVancomycin + an antipseudomonal β-lactam (cefepime 2 g q8h) is the sensible shocked-patient regimen. Load vancomycin at 25–30 mg/kg actual body weight — the loading dose matters far more in shock than the maintenance dose, and it is the step most often skipped.
Crystalloid30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 hUse balanced solution rather than 0.9% saline. Reassess dynamically — do not give the full 30 mL/kg reflexively to a patient with heart failure or established renal failure.
VasopressorsMAP ≥65 mmHgStart norepinephrine peripherally through a good line while central access is obtained rather than tolerating a period of hypotension.
LactateMeasure and repeat if >2A lactate that will not clear in a septic arthritis patient is a source-control question first and a haemodynamic question second.
SOURCE CONTROLDrainage as soon as feasible — within 24 h at the outside, immediately if shockedThe element that is unique to this disease and the one most often deferred. Call the surgeon during the resuscitation, not after it.
Give the vancomycin loading dose. A patient started on 1 g q12h without a load spends 24–48 hours subtherapeutic — precisely the window when the bacterial burden is highest. Load 25–30 mg/kg actual body weight (max 3 g), then dose maintenance from creatinine, then let pharmacy chase the AUC. Target AUC₂₄ 400–600 mg·h/L.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs and targets

ItemWhenWhy / target
Arterial lineAny patient on vasopressors, or needing frequent gasesBeat-to-beat MAP for a target of ≥65 mmHg, and painless repeated sampling.
Central venous accessVasopressors beyond a short peripheral run; multiple incompatible infusions; poor peripheral accessReliable vasopressor delivery. Avoid the femoral site if there is a septic hip or groin — do not run a line through infected tissue.
Urinary catheterShock, or needing hourly urine outputTarget >0.5 mL/kg/h. Remove as soon as it is not needed.
LactateOn arrival, then every 2–4 h until clearingClearance is the resuscitation endpoint that best tracks outcome. Failure to clear = re-examine the source.
CRPDailyShould fall and normalise within about a week. A slow fall by post-operative day 3 and day 5 is specifically linked to treatment failure and the need for further surgery.
Blood culturesRepeat every 48 h until negative if initially positivePersistent S. aureus bacteraemia beyond 72 h means another focus — echocardiogram, spine and joint imaging, and remove every line you can.
Vancomycin levelsPer pharmacy, AUC-guidedAUC₂₄/MIC 400–600 mg·h/L. Nephrotoxicity risk rises above roughly 650.
Creatinine, electrolytes, LFTs, FBC, coagulationDaily minimumAKI is common and multifactorial — sepsis, hypotension, vancomycin, NSAIDs, contrast. Review the whole chart daily for stacked nephrotoxins.
CKDaily if on daptomycinMyopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Hold statins while on daptomycin.
EchocardiogramAny S. aureus bacteraemia, polyarticular disease, IVDU, murmur, prosthetic valve or deviceTTE first; TOE if TTE is negative and suspicion persists — TTE misses a substantial minority of vegetations.
Whole-body or targeted imagingIf persistently bacteraemic or not improvingLook for metastatic foci: a second joint, vertebral osteomyelitis, psoas or epidural abscess, splenic or renal abscess. S. aureus seeds widely and quietly.
GlucoseHourly to 4-hourly on insulin infusionTarget roughly 140–180 mg/dL (7.8–10 mmol/L). Avoid hypoglycaemia — it is more dangerous here than mild hyperglycaemia.
Support

Pressors & inotropes

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Septic shock here is distributive — cytokine-driven vasodilation with inducible nitric oxide synthase upregulation and vasopressin depletion. So the primary target is α₁-mediated vasoconstriction, not inotropy. Reach for an inotrope only when you have evidence of genuine pump failure (septic cardiomyopathy), because giving inotropes to a vasodilated patient just adds tachyarrhythmia.
AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHaemodynamic effectWhen to pick it
Norepinephrine
FIRST LINE		α₁ ≫ β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min; titrate every 2–5 min to MAP ≥65. Doses >0.5 are used but should trigger adding a second agent.↑↑ SVR, modest ↑ CO, minimal ↑ HR relative to its pressor effectFirst line in every septic shock, including this one. Start peripherally through a good line rather than tolerating hypotension while you get central access.
Vasopressin
second agent		V₁ receptors — a non-adrenergic pathway entirely0.03 units/min fixed (some use up to 0.04). Not titrated.↑ SVR without β stimulation; no tachycardiaAdd when norepinephrine reaches roughly 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min. Because it works through a different receptor, it is genuinely catecholamine-sparing — and endogenous vasopressin is depleted in prolonged shock.
Epinephrineα₁, β₁, β₂0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ SVR, ↑↑ CO, ↑↑ HRThird line, or when septic cardiomyopathy means you need inotropy and vasoconstriction together. Expect lactate to rise from β₂-driven glycolysis — that is pharmacological, not worsening perfusion, and misreading it leads to over-resuscitation.
PhenylephrinePure α₁0.5–9 mcg/kg/min (or boluses 50–200 mcg)↑ SVR, reflex ↓ HR, may ↓ CONiche: when tachyarrhythmia genuinely prohibits norepinephrine. Reflex bradycardia and reduced cardiac output make it a poor default.
Dobutamineβ₁ > β₂2.5–20 mcg/kg/min↑↑ CO, ↓ SVR, ↑ HROnly for demonstrated septic cardiomyopathy — echo showing poor contractility with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP and filling. It will drop the blood pressure, so it goes alongside norepinephrine, never instead of it.
Angiotensin IIAT₁ receptor — a third independent vasoconstrictor pathway20 ng/kg/min, titrate to 80; up to 200 briefly↑↑ SVRRefractory vasodilatory shock on maximal norepinephrine plus vasopressin. Adds a third receptor pathway. Thrombosis risk — VTE prophylaxis matters.
HydrocortisoneRestores adrenergic receptor sensitivity; genomic and non-genomic vascular effects200 mg/day IV — 50 mg q6h or continuous infusionReduces vasopressor durationRefractory shock requiring ongoing vasopressors. Note this is a distinct question from adjunctive steroid for the joint itself — here you are treating shock, and that indication is well established.
Adjunctive corticosteroid for the JOINT is a different question — and the honest answer is that adult evidence is thin. The mechanistic rationale is good: dampen the neutrophil and cytokine cascade that is doing most of the cartilage damage. Two placebo-controlled paediatric RCTs support it — Odio 2003 (n=149; dexamethasone reduced residual joint dysfunction at 12 months and shortened symptoms by a mean 5.47 days) and Harel 2011 (n=49; shorter fever and inflammation, lower acute-phase reactants, shorter parenteral antibiotic course). There is no adequately powered adult RCT, and BSAC has explicitly flagged that clinicians may be using steroids in adults without an adequate evidence base. Do not extrapolate the paediatric data to routine adult practice. Hydrocortisone for refractory shock is a separate, well-supported indication.
Airway

Respiratory support

🌬️

When to intubate, and the initial settings

Septic arthritis does not cause respiratory failure by itself. When a patient needs the ventilator, it is because of ARDS from sepsis, septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided endocarditis (think of this in every patient who injects drugs), concurrent pneumonia, fluid overload from resuscitation, or the need for general anaesthesia for repeated washouts.

EscalationUse it whenDo not use it when
Nasal cannula / face maskMild hypoxaemia, SpO₂ target 92–96%Rising work of breathing
High-flow nasal oxygenHypoxaemic failure without hypercapnia; comfortable, allows talking and eatingDepressed consciousness, or persistent hypercapnia
NIV (BiPAP)Hypercapnic failure, coexisting COPD, or cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from over-resuscitationDepressed GCS, vomiting, haemodynamic instability, or as a way of postponing an intubation that is clearly needed. NIV in a shocked septic patient with ARDS delays the inevitable and worsens it.
IntubationRefractory hypoxaemia, exhaustion, GCS decline, airway protection, or elective intubation for theatre in an unstable patient—

Initial ventilator settings — lung-protective from the first breath

Mode
AC/VC
volume control, assist-control
Tidal volume
6 mL/kg IBW
predicted body weight from HEIGHT, never actual weight
PEEP
5–10 cmH₂O
titrate up for oxygenation; higher if ARDS
FiO₂
100% → wean
target SpO₂ 92–96%, PaO₂ 55–80 mmHg
Rate
16–24/min
higher to compensate the metabolic acidosis of sepsis
Plateau pressure
< 30 cmH₂O
check with an inspiratory hold q4h and after any change
Driving pressure
< 15 cmH₂O
plateau minus PEEP — tracks outcome better than either alone
pH target
> 7.25
permissive hypercapnia is acceptable
In a patient who injects drugs with a septic sternoclavicular or sacroiliac joint and unexplained hypoxaemia, get a CT pulmonary angiogram and an echocardiogram. Right-sided endocarditis showering septic emboli into the lungs is a classic and frequently missed combination — and it changes both the antibiotic duration and the surgical conversation.
If you are ventilating a septic arthritis patient and they are not improving, ask whether the joint has actually been drained. It is remarkably easy for a joint to become a footnote once a patient is intubated on three organ supports — and it is still the source.
Rescue

Advanced & refractory options

⚙️

When standard therapy is failing

1
Re-interrogate source control — always first
Before you escalate anything pharmacological
▾

The overwhelming majority of "refractory septic arthritis" is inadequately drained septic arthritis. Work through this list before adding drugs:

  • Re-examine the joint yourself. Is it tense again?
  • Repeat imaging — MRI or CT for a loculated collection, an adjacent abscess, or osteomyelitis that was missed.
  • Back to theatre. Around 25% of arthroscopically treated patients need more than one lavage, and compromised hosts had >16× the failure risk after a single washout. A second look is normal practice, not an admission of failure.
  • Look for a second focus — another joint, endocarditis, vertebral osteomyelitis, psoas or epidural abscess, an infected line.
  • Remove every removable line and any retained foreign body.
Escalating antibiotics in place of re-draining a joint is the classic error of this disease at every level of care. If the CRP is not falling by day 3–5, the answer is usually surgical.
2
Re-interrogate the microbiology
Is the organism what you think it is?
▾
  • Re-culture the joint and the blood. Ask the laboratory to hold cultures longer.
  • Broaden the differential: mycobacteria, fungi (Candida in the ICU patient with lines and TPN), Nocardia, Brucella. Send AFB and fungal cultures and consider synovial biopsy rather than repeat aspiration.
  • 16S rRNA PCR or metagenomic sequencing on synovial fluid — sensitivity for the latter has been reported around 88.5%, and it is most useful exactly here, in the culture-negative non-responder.
  • Check the MIC. Vancomycin MIC ≥2 mg/L predicts failure — change agent rather than pushing the dose into nephrotoxic territory.
  • Check the D-test if you are relying on clindamycin, and confirm you are actually achieving your vancomycin AUC target.
  • Consider drug fever and C. difficile as non-joint explanations for persistent fever.
3
Salvage antimicrobial strategies
ID-directed, not empiric
▾
OptionDoseWhenCaveat
Daptomycin high-dose8–10 mg/kg IV q24hMRSA failing vancomycin, vancomycin MIC ≥2, or vancomycin-induced AKICK weekly; hold statins; watch for eosinophilic pneumonia
Ceftaroline600 mg IV q12hMRSA salvage — the only cephalosporin with PBP2a affinity; sometimes combined with daptomycin in refractory MRSA bacteraemiaOff-label for osteoarticular infection; neutropenia with prolonged use
Linezolid600 mg IV/PO q12hMRSA/VRE; excellent tissue penetration; useful when renal function forbids vancomycinCytopenias, neuropathy beyond 2–4 weeks, MAOI interactions
Ceftazidime-avibactam / meropenem-vaborbactam / ceftolozane-tazobactamPer ID and local susceptibilitiesCarbapenem-resistant or difficult-to-treat resistant gram-negativesStrictly ID-directed; needs susceptibility confirmation
Antifungal (echinocandin, then fluconazole if susceptible)e.g. caspofungin 70 mg load then 50 mg IV dailyCandida arthritis — the ICU patient with lines, TPN, prior broad-spectrum antibiotics, or who injects drugsProlonged course; almost always needs surgical debridement too
4
Organ support & last-resort measures
And the honest conversation
▾
  • Renal replacement therapy for refractory AKI. Critically, antibiotic dosing changes substantially on RRT — vancomycin and β-lactam regimens must be redone with pharmacy, and under-dosing on CRRT is a common and silent cause of treatment failure.
  • VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock from severe septic cardiomyopathy — rare, centre-dependent, and only in a patient with a survivable underlying problem.
  • Amputation or resection arthroplasty — genuinely last-resort for uncontrollable infection in a destroyed joint, most often the diabetic foot or a catastrophic prosthetic infection. It is a life-saving operation when it is needed and should not be delayed by optimism.
  • Goals-of-care discussion. This is a rescue option, not a failure. Mortality in the over-80s has been reported as high as 22–69%, and polyarticular disease in a frail RA patient carries figures around 40–50%. A frail patient facing repeated washouts, prolonged ICU care and a permanently non-functional joint deserves an explicit, early conversation about what they would want — held alongside active treatment, not only after it fails.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

There is no validated septic-arthritis-specific downgrade protocol in the literature — these are general sepsis-resolution criteria plus the source-control questions that are specific to this disease. Both halves matter.
DomainReady to downgrade when
HaemodynamicsOff all vasopressors ≥6–12 h with MAP ≥65 mmHg maintained unsupported; heart rate controlled
PerfusionLactate normalised (<2 mmol/L) and staying down; urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h
Source controlThe joint has been definitively drained, is not reaccumulating on examination, and no further washout is planned in the next 24 h
RespiratoryExtubated ≥12–24 h without distress, or on ≤4 L nasal oxygen with SpO₂ ≥92%
NeurologicalAwake, oriented, or back to documented baseline; delirium settled or manageable on the floor
Renal / metabolicCreatinine stable or improving; no RRT need; electrolytes and acid-base corrected
Infection trajectoryAfebrile ≥24 h; CRP falling convincingly; blood cultures negative
PlanDefinitive organism-directed regimen with a stop date; ID and orthopaedics engaged; physiotherapy underway
Not yet — even if the numbers look acceptable — if: the joint has not been definitively drained or another washout is planned; blood cultures are still positive; the CRP is plateaued or rising (the day 3–5 trajectory is a validated warning sign for failure and further surgery); vasopressors were stopped within the last few hours; S. aureus bacteraemia is not yet explained by a completed echocardiogram; a new joint has become symptomatic; or the patient needs anaesthesia again in the next 24 hours. Downgrading a patient who then needs re-escalation carries worse outcomes than keeping them one more night.

ICU disposition

Ward / step-down

Shock resolved, source controlled, on a definitive antibiotic plan. The great majority.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Significant functional loss after prolonged ICU stay or large-joint destruction, but ≥3 h therapy/day tolerable across ≥2 disciplines with real rehabilitation potential.

SNF

Needs 24-hour skilled nursing plus ongoing IV therapy but cannot tolerate intensive rehabilitation. Common in the frail elderly.

LTAC

Prolonged ventilator weaning, serial washouts, complex wounds, or extended IV therapy in a medically fragile patient — anticipated >25 days.

Palliative / hospice

Multi-organ failure not responding to source control in a frail patient; polyarticular sepsis with mortality figures around 40–50%; or a patient whose stated goals do not include repeated surgery. Antibiotics can continue as symptom control.
Pearls

Clinical pearls

💡

Twenty things worth knowing before you next see a hot joint

  1. No synovial cell count rules the diagnosis in or out. Even >100,000/mm³ carries a likelihood ratio of 28, not infinity — and <25,000 carries an LR of 0.32, which on a 40% pretest probability still leaves you around 18%. Margaretten's own conclusion was that no cut-off excludes septic arthritis.
  2. Crystals and infection coexist in up to 21% of surgically treated series. Finding urate or pyrophosphate crystals does not end the investigation — and crystal disease is itself a risk factor for infection.
  3. A normal CRP or ESR does not exclude it, and neither does a normal white count — leukocytosis is present in only about half of cases. Serum markers have likelihood ratios of just 1.3–1.6. They barely move the needle.
  4. Roughly 4 in 10 patients are afebrile. Fever has a sensitivity of about 57%. The absence of fever is one of the least useful negative findings in medicine here.
  5. The RA patient on a TNF inhibitor is the classic miss. Adjusted hazard ratio 2.3 for septic arthritis, RA patients make up around 20% of all cases, and the drug removes the fever that would have prompted the tap. A single acutely hot joint in this patient is aspirated, not observed.
  6. Do not give antibiotics before aspirating unless the patient is septic. Prior antibiotics drop Gram-stain sensitivity from roughly 58% to 12% and culture from 79% to 28%. You cannot get that information back.
  7. The hip is a surgical emergency, full stop. The femoral head's blood supply runs inside the capsule, so a tense effusion causes avascular necrosis. Needle aspiration is a diagnostic step on the way to theatre, not an alternative to it.
  8. Gonococcal joint cultures are usually negative. Send NAATs from urethral/cervical, pharyngeal and rectal sites regardless of local symptoms — and screen for HIV and syphilis while you are there.
  9. Polyarticular disease is a mortality red flag, with reported figures of 32–50% versus about 11% for monoarticular. It also means sustained bacteraemia: get an echocardiogram and find the source.
  10. Sternoclavicular joint infection in someone who injects drugs needs a CT before anyone touches it — retrosternal and mediastinal extension is common and changes the operation and the team.
  11. Prosthetic joints are a different disease. Different organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium), a diagnostic cell-count threshold an order of magnitude lower, and a DAIR-versus-exchange algorithm. Do not aspirate one on the ward, and never apply native-joint short courses to it.
  12. Kocher criteria performed worse on validation than derivation — 99.6% dropped to 93% at 4/4, and <0.2% rose to 2% at 0/4. Worse, Kingella kingae in under-4s often produces an indolent illness with a near-normal CRP that defeats the score entirely. Use it to support aspiration, never to avoid it.
  13. Kingella is easily missed on standard plating. Inoculate synovial fluid directly into a blood-culture bottle, or send PCR — one series recovered the organism on culture in only 2 of 27 PCR-positive samples.
  14. The destruction is mostly host-mediated. Neutrophil elastase, MMP-1/3/13 and free radicals do more damage than the bacteria. That single fact is why drainage is a co-equal partner to antibiotics and not an afterthought — and why "started on IV antibiotics, review tomorrow" is inadequate.
  15. Intra-articular antibiotics have no role and cause chemical synovitis. Systemic dosing already achieves good synovial concentrations because inflamed synovium is highly permeable — which is also why "the drug can't get in" is not a valid explanation for failure in a native joint.
  16. Duration is genuinely unsettled, and the deciding variable is source control, not the calendar. Gjika 2019 found 2 weeks non-inferior to 4 after surgical drainage — but 64% of that cohort were hand and wrist joints. A large-joint cohort found antibiotics ≤4 weeks associated with relapse (OR 25.47). Match the duration to the joint, the organism and the adequacy of drainage.
  17. OVIVA killed the "six weeks of IV" dogma for bone and joint infection generally — oral was non-inferior, with catheter complications of 0.96% versus 9.37%. But its population was mostly osteomyelitis and prosthetic joints, so cite it for the route, not as septic-arthritis-specific duration evidence.
  18. CRP trajectory is your best early-warning system. It normalises within about a week of effective treatment, and a slow fall at post-operative day 3 and day 5 is specifically associated with treatment failure and the need for further surgery. A slowly falling CRP is an actionable finding, not a number to note.
  19. MRSA septic arthritis skews dramatically older and sicker — mean age 76 versus 44 for MSSA in one cohort, with treatment failure 33.3% versus 11.3%. A positive MRSA nasal screen was present in 51% of MRSA cases versus 5.6% of MSSA cases, which genuinely helps refine empiric choices.
  20. Start moving the joint on day 1. Around 39% of patients have mechanical sequelae, dominated by stiffness and adhesions. Cartilage is nourished by cyclical loading and denuded surfaces adhere quickly. The joint needs rest from weight-bearing, not immobility.

Landmark trials & studies — what they showed and why they matter

StudyYearDesign / NResultWhy it matters
Margaretten et al.
JAMA Rational Clinical Exam		2007 Systematic review, 14 studies Synovial WBC likelihood ratios 2.9 / 7.7 / 28 at 25k / 50k / 100k; PMN ≥90% LR 3.4, <90% LR 0.34; serum WBC, ESR and CRP LR only 1.3–1.6 The core evidence base for reading synovial fluid. Its central message — that no cut-off excludes the diagnosis — is the single most important idea in the disease and the one most often forgotten at 3am.
Kaandorp et al.
Arthritis Rheum		1995 Prospective cohort, 4,907 rheumatic-disease patients over 3 years (37 cases) Odds ratios: skin infection 27.2, prosthesis 15, joint surgery 5.1, RA 4.0, age ≥80 3.5, diabetes 3.3 The best-quantified risk-factor dataset in the field. Note that the strongest risk factor is also the most modifiable — treating skin infection is septic arthritis prevention.
Weston et al.
Ann Rheum Dis, Nottingham UK		1999 Retrospective, single UK health district, 1982–1991 Mortality 11.5%, morbidity 31.6%. Independent predictors of death: confusion at presentation, age ≥65, multiple-joint sepsis or elbow involvement. Predictors of morbidity: age ≥65, diabetes, open drainage, gram-positive organism other than S. aureus Foundational outcome dataset, and the source of the prognostic factors still quoted. Its "open drainage predicts morbidity" finding is a teaching example of confounding by indication — the worst joints got opened.
Gjika et al.
Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:1114–21		2019 Prospective randomised non-inferiority RCT, n=154 (77 per arm), adults, after surgical lavage 2 weeks non-inferior to 4 weeks — remission 76/77 vs 75/77; recurrence 1 vs 2 (p=0.58); adverse events 3% vs 6%; hospital stay 4 vs 6 days (p=0.01). Median IV duration only 1–2 days. Sequelae 39% overall, and the sequelae endpoint did not meet non-inferiority The most directly applicable duration RCT in native joint disease. Read the population before you generalise: 64% were hand and wrist joints, and the authors framed the conclusion as holding "at least for hand and wrist arthritis."
Korean native-joint cohort
culture-positive NJSA, 2004–2020		2023 Retrospective cohort, n=137, mostly large joints, median follow-up 2.7 years Overall relapse 9.5%. Antibiotics ≤4 weeks → OR 25.47 for relapse (95% CI 1.57–412.33). Synovial WBC ≥150,000 → OR 17.46. S. aureus 65.7% (MRSA 19.7%) The essential counterweight to Gjika. Short courses that work for hand and wrist joints may not transfer to a knee or shoulder. The wide confidence interval reflects small numbers, but the direction is consistent — and this is the population you usually have on the ward.
OVIVA (Li et al.)
N Engl J Med 2019;380:425–36		2019 Multicentre open-label non-inferiority RCT, n=1,054, 26 UK hospitals Oral non-inferior to IV for the first 6 weeks of complex bone/joint infection — risk difference −1.38% (90% CI −4.94 to +2.19). Catheter complications 0.96% oral vs 9.37% IV; ~£2,740 saved per patient Destroyed the dogma that bone and joint infection mandates six weeks of IV therapy. Applicability caveat: the population was overwhelmingly osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint and diabetic foot infection — cite it for the route, not as septic-arthritis-specific.
Kocher et al.
JBJS Am 1999;81:1662–70		1999 Retrospective derivation, n=282 (82 with septic arthritis) Four predictors (fever >38.5 °C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12,000) → probability <0.2% / 3.0% / 40% / 93.1% / 99.6% for 0–4 criteria Defined the paediatric hip prediction rule still in daily use.
Kocher et al. validation
JBJS Am 2004;86:1629–35		2004 Prospective external validation, 51 septic arthritis vs 103 transient synovitis Probability fell to 2% / 9.5% / 35% / 72.8% / 93% for 0–4 criteria A masterclass in why prediction rules degrade outside their derivation cohort. Also the reason Kocher must never be used to avoid an aspiration.
Peltola et al.
Clin Infect Dis 2009;48:1201		2009 Prospective multicentre RCT, Finland, culture-positive childhood septic arthritis 10 days non-inferior to 30 days with early IV-to-oral switch; a single aspiration was usually sufficient Foundational paediatric short-course evidence, and the earliest strong signal that the field had been over-treating.
Odio et al.
Pediatr Infect Dis J		2003 Double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=149 children Adjunctive IV dexamethasone reduced residual joint dysfunction at 12 months and shortened symptom duration by a mean of 5.47 days First strong evidence for adjunctive steroid — mechanistically satisfying given that the damage is host-mediated. Paediatric only.
Harel et al.
J Pediatr Orthop		2011 Double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=49 children Dexamethasone shortened fever and inflammation, lowered acute-phase reactants, shortened parenteral antibiotic duration Confirmatory paediatric steroid RCT. Adult evidence remains sparse — BSAC has explicitly flagged that adults may be receiving steroids without an adequate evidence base.
Ravindran et al.
Rheumatology		2009 Retrospective, single UK centre, 6 years: 32 needle aspiration vs 19 surgical drainage No baseline comorbidity difference between the medical and surgical groups One of very few direct medical-versus-surgical comparisons. It does not settle the question — which is itself the point: the aspiration-versus-washout debate rests on weak comparative evidence.
Surgical delay cohort
Open Forum Infect Dis		2025 Outcomes analysis of delay to surgical intervention Longer delay → 1-year mortality HR 1.7 (95% CI 1.1–2.6, p=0.019) and treatment failure HR 1.5 (95% CI 1.1–2.0, p=0.007), persisting after adjustment for age and Charlson index. At 1 year, 57% full recovery, 34% treatment failure The best modern quantification of why "we'll do it on tomorrow's list" is not a neutral decision.
Galloway et al. (BSRBR)
British Society for Rheumatology Biologics Register		2011 National biologics registry cohort, RA patients Septic arthritis 4.2 vs 1.8 per 1,000 patient-years; unadjusted HR 2.5 (1.6–4.0), adjusted HR 2.3 (1.2–4.4) for anti-TNF vs non-biologic DMARDs The best-quantified biologic-specific risk data, and the numeric basis for maintaining a very low aspiration threshold in this group.
Arthroscopy vs arthrotomy meta-analysis2020s Systematic review / meta-analysis of native joints Comparable infection-eradication rates between arthroscopic lavage and open arthrotomy Supports arthroscopy as at least equivalent and less morbid — now the usual first surgical choice for accessible large joints.
Procalcitonin meta-analysis2017 Meta-analysis, 10 studies, 838 patients Sensitivity 54% (41–66), specificity 95% (87–98), LR+ 10.97, LR− 0.49, AUC 0.82 Settles how to use procalcitonin here: helpful to rule in, useless to rule out. There is no blood test that lets you skip the aspiration.

Accuracy notes — read these

Several figures commonly quoted for this disease could not be traced to a primary source, and are deliberately not stated as fact anywhere in this guide:

  • "Irreversible cartilage damage within 8 hours." No primary citation was found. The verified experimental trajectory (rabbit knee, bovine explant) is ~42% glycosaminoglycan loss at 48 h, marginal erosion by day 5, ~73% loss by week 3, total destruction by ~week 5 — which supports the same urgency without inventing a number.
  • Synovial total lactate ">10 mmol/L". The underlying studies frequently did not state whether D- or L-lactate was measured. Modern D-lactate data (cut-off ~0.033–0.04 mmol/L, sensitivity 90–92%, specificity 83–85%) is quoted instead.
  • Exact percentage of cases attributable to the haematogenous route. Described qualitatively as the dominant route; no clean pooled figure exists.
  • Ceftriaxone q12h vs q24h for non-gonococcal septic arthritis. 2 g once daily is well supported; the q12h practice seen at some centres is not reconciled by a single authoritative guideline — confirm locally.
  • A numeric "day X" threshold for declaring serial needle aspiration a failure. None is validated; the escalation criteria given are synthesised from the literature and are deliberately clinical rather than numeric.
  • Timing for resuming biologic/DMARD therapy after treated septic arthritis. No validated interval exists — this is a rheumatology/ID co-management decision.
  • Pregnancy-specific septic arthritis data. No quantified body of evidence identified; manage per general pregnancy-safe antimicrobial principles with obstetric involvement.

This guide is an educational reference for clinicians in training. It is not a substitute for local antimicrobial guidelines, current guideline texts, or specialist advice. Verify every dose against your own formulary and renal-dosing reference before prescribing. Guidelines and USPSTF recommendations are updated periodically — check the primary sources above for the current version.
